‘Does my vote really count?’ Morocco’s Gen Z weigh hope against disillusionment ahead of election Submitted by Caroline Dupuy on Tue, 09/08/2026 - 11:58 As general elections approach, young voters who took to the streets a year ago remain wary of corruption and broken promises A protester from Generation Z holds a sign reading “Stop the high prices, people’s pockets are empty” during a demonstration in front of the Moroccan parliament in Rabat on 9 October 2025 (Issam Zerrok/Hans Lucas/Reuters) Off Morocco is gearing up for its general election on 23 September to determine who will form the next government and replace the current prime minister, billionaire tycoon Aziz Akhannouch , elected in September 2021. Over the last year alone, Morocco has faced a turbulent political landscape, from the Gen Z protests in September 2025 to the latest migrant crisis, with 72,000 Moroccans entering the Spanish enclave of Ceuta at the end of July. The vote comes one year after the so-called Gen Z 212 uprising, when young people mobilised on Discord after eight women died within several days following routine caesarean sections in a public hospital in Agadir. The movement quickly built momentum and morphed into wider calls for better education infrastructure, calling on the government to prioritise spending in critical areas rather than stadiums for Morocco’s co-hosting of the 2030 World Cup. Morocco has a young population, with over 50 percent of the country under 35 years old. Most of those participating in the Gen Z movement and mass migration attempt to Ceuta were young Moroccans, meaning a significant portion of the country's youth is entering this election cycle politically active yet deeply disillusioned. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Jihane*, a political coordinator at a Moroccan youth centre, told Middle East Eye “this upcoming election is particularly interesting because more young people appear to be engaged, and many are encouraging one another to vote”. Despite youth engagement, many remain unsure that voting will have any real impact on their situation, while fears of corruption linger. “There is still considerable debate among youth. Many continue to ask: does my vote really count?” Jihane said. The young woman senses what she describes as “cautious optimism”. ‘It is almost as if they are saying, “we'll trust you once more, but will you betray that trust again?”’ - Jihane, political coordinator Many young people are seemingly willing to give the political process another chance, she said. “It is almost as if they are saying, 'we'll trust you once more, but will you betray that trust again?’” For Hassan, a journalist and activist in the Gen Z protests and Discord network, the Ceuta migrant crisis, which consisted mostly of young Moroccans, was a statement from this generation. "We no longer want to be part of this farce. We’ve lost hope in the parties or the state to represent us and our hopes and aspirations,” he told MEE, calling the border crossing a “collective scream from all Moroccans” and not only from the youth. Hassan believes “Gen Z see no point in holding elections”. He cited the silence from government officials when the protests were brutally suppressed . During the events, three people were killed and at least 2,400 were arrested; around 600 people are still in prison. “The system has proved that it would rather see us die in the sea than respond to our smallest demands,” he said. Many observers accuse Morocco of engineering the Ceuta crisis to pressure Spain. An investigation has been opened in Spain after a police report described Moroccan law enforcement as broadly permissive and even facilitating the mass crossing. Rabat has denied any involvement. A World Cup government Accusations of political poaching and corruption emerging between parties are doing little to reassure young voters. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); The current party in power, the centre-right National Rally of Independents (RNI), recently accused the liberal Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM) of “undermining the ethics of political work and the rules of sound democratic competition”. 'Morocco has given me nothing': The young migrants risking everything to reach Ceuta Read More » RNI is the main leading party in power, but PAM, one of the country’s largest political parties, is a strong contender to become the next leading party. RNI won 97 out of the 395 seats in the 2021 elections and PAM had 82. The statements stem from a leaked recording of an RNI meeting where the House of Representatives and senior RNI member Rachid Talbi Alami is heard talking about corruption and political poaching at PAM, critically mentioning the minister delegate in charge of the budget, Fouzi Lekjaa. The comments come after Lekjaa, who also serves as president of the Royal Football Federation and until recently had no party affiliation, joined PAM a month ahead of the elections. In response, PAM said that politicians joining the party had done so freely, rejecting RNI's claims of coercion. However, speculation has mounted that this strategic move is designed to position Lekjaa as the next prime minister. Given his dual influence in finance and football, analysts are describing the manoeuvre as the foundation for a World Cup government, a political strategy tailored to lead Morocco as it prepares to co-host the 2030 tournament. ‘We’ve lost hope in the parties or the state to represent us and our hopes and aspirations’ - Hassan, journalist and activist Hassan called the Lekjaa move “a joker card pulled by the Makhzen deep state”, referring to the name given to Morocco’s royal‑centred political establishment. The Morocco 2030 Foundation, created to oversee the World Cup and Africa Cup of Nations hosting, “is the real next government,” the activist said. The election process has also cast doubt over the likelihood of a true democratic process. For the upcoming vote, the interior ministry, which only answers to the king, has taken on a supervisory role in the electoral process. “This adds insult to injury,” Hassan told MEE. “In the past, the ministry’s role was behind the scenes in playing with the ballots, now it is very direct.” Superficial reforms Following on from Gen Z demands, the Moroccan government created a new initiative to financially assist young people in campaigning and to promote youth participation in government by covering 75 percent of campaign costs. Submitted by MEE correspondent on Mon, 09/14/2026 - 09:37 After seizing the entire Red Sea coast, the Houthis are attempting to advance into western Taiz Yemen's Houthi armed forces patrol as freed prisoners loyal to the Ansar Allah authorities arrive in the capital Sanaa on 12 September 2026 (Mohammed Huwais / AFP) Off On 3 September, Houthi forces launched a heavy offensive against Yemen's internationally recognised government in the southern Hodeidah districts of Hays and Al-Khawkha, as well as the western Taiz districts of Jabal Habashi, Maqbana, Mowza’a, and Al-Wazeyaha. These areas form a crucial geographic corridor that connects the mountainous highlands of Taiz to the coastal plain along the Red Sea. Government forces initially repelled the attacks across both governorates, halting the Houthi advance toward Mocha for nearly a week - however, on Wednesday night, Houthi fighters launched a rapid assault from southern Hodeidah and western Taiz, capturing Mocha in a single night. Government units - including the National Resistance Forces (NRF), the Nation’s Shield Forces (NSF), and the Giants Brigades (Al-Amaliqah) - attempted to push back, but were ultimately seen retreating from Mocha toward Bab al-Mandab and Lahj governorate. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); By the following morning, Houthi forces had advanced to capture the Bab al-Mandab Strait and Mayyun Island - the strategic focal point overseeing the strait - as government troops withdrew toward the Ras al-A'ara area in Lahj. Throughout the battles in Hodeidah and Taiz, the Houthis consistently maintained the offensive, leaving government forces mostly on the defensive - holding ground in some sectors while failing in others. Since Friday, the Houthis have targeted government positions past Bab al-Mandab with multiple missile strikes. However, the fiercest clashes remain centred on the western Taiz fronts, where Houthi troops continue pushing to secure additional areas across the governorate. What happened on the Red Sea coast? “We fought the Houthis for a week, but they received continuous reinforcements and relentless support from ground and air forces,” a fighter who took part in the battles told Middle East Eye. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); “We were divided into separate units, with each group taking orders from its own commander, leaving us scattered across the battlefield.” 'I am not trying to blame anyone, but when one group pulled back, the rest followed suit' - pro-government fighter He emphasised that his unit did not retreat at the onset, holding their ground for a full week before withdrawing only “when it became impossible to stay”. “I am deeply hurt by the criticism directed at us. We were accused of fleeing by people who have no idea what actual battle entails,” the fighter added. He explained that while units attempted to coordinate under fragmented leadership, deteriorating communication during the heaviest fighting eventually triggered the retreat. “I am not trying to blame anyone, but when one group pulled back, the rest followed suit. We retreated to Mocha, and from there toward Bab al-Mandab and Ras al-A'ara,” said the fighter, who spoke to MEE after successfully escaping Mocha for Aden. While clashes have broken out across multiple governorates - including Al-Jawf, Al-Bayda, Marib, Al-Dhale, Hodeidah, and Taiz - the most severe engagements remain concentrated in the latter. In response, the Yemeni Armed Forces announced they will deploy all available ground and air assets to target Houthi movements within an operational zone spanning the Taiz–Mocha road, Jabal al-Nar, and Mocha, releasing a target map alongside the statement. ‘Like a battlefield’: How Yemen’s Mocha went from a town of fishermen to a city of fighters Read More » On 10 September, official military spokesperson Colonel Majed al-Nuzaili urged civilians to avoid the Taiz–Mocha road until further notice and to stay clear of Houthi military concentrations. Government forces have since launched air strikes against Houthi positions in Mocha and along the western coast to support a push to retake the city, though no territorial ground gains have yet been achieved. Houthi officials accused Saudi Arabia of conducting over 100 air strikes across Yemen within a 48-hour window, though Saudi authorities have not claimed responsibility for the operations. Meanwhile, the National Resistance Forces reported significant casualties from the recent offensive, confirming that over 500 of their fighters were killed and more than 1,500 wounded According to the International Organization for Migration's (IOM) more than 82,000 were displaced since the beginning of September as fighting continues along the west coast. Families are being forced from their homes, and some are now fleeing the country altogether. IOM stated that over 2,000 people fleeing the hostilities have reached Djibouti's northern shores so far, landing at scattered points along the coast near Obock. Recapturing coastal areas Although the Yemeni government announced plans to target Houthi positions, the morale of pro-government supporters who withdrew from the west coast remains severely battered, making it difficult to halt further Houthi advances in the immediate term. Professor Abdulsattar al-Shamiri, a Yemeni political analyst and CEO of the Johood Center for Studies and Research, attributed the setback to a distinct lack of coordination among military factions, which ultimately led to the defeat of government forces. 'If the Houthis manage to consolidate their presence in Mocha and Bab al-Mandab, they will gain massive strategic leverage against Saudi Arabia, the United States, and international powers' - Dr Mohammed al-Shuaibi, University of Aden "There are no explicit disagreements in the literal sense, but there are clear discrepancies in coordination methods," he told MEE. "As for the setback that occurred in Mocha and the rest of the coastal areas, it stems from central factors - chief among them weak command and control, as the command structure within the Yemeni army units was not functioning as it should." Shamiri noted additional factors that undermined government forces, including a lack of effective air cover. The air force failed to intervene with the same scale and impact seen a decade ago, when the Saudi-led coalition actively supported ground forces across Yemen. “Supply shortages, rapid rearmament crises, and poor communication are considered other causes, along with the absence of central oversight,” Shamiri added. Despite detailing the reasons behind the military loss, Shamiri expressed confidence that Yemeni forces could eventually reclaim lost areas. “Recapturing areas is possible, but it will not be easy or quick. It will require organised effort, high readiness, and more time - especially given that these areas were previously under Houthi control before they were forcefully expelled,” he explained. Shamiri added that the coming phase will likely depend on a strategy of deep attrition, utilising targeted air strikes and surgical ground operations against Houthi strongholds. “This attrition may force them to withdraw from certain areas, despite Iran having secured a major strategic gain and potentially pushing further support to the Houthis,” he said. “The government forces are, therefore, facing a long-term war of attrition.” (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Dr Mohammed al-Shuaibi, professor of strategic planning at the University of Aden, similarly believes that recapturing coastal areas along the Red Sea remains achievable if forces realign. “The government forces can unify their leadership and militarily recapture Mocha,” he told MEE. “To achieve this, it requires forming a unified operations room, a single political decision, and subsequently selecting a unified field command - specifically from among those leaders who enjoy acceptance and possess sufficient battleground experience there.” Intermediate objective By seizing positions along Yemen’s Red Sea coast - such as Mocha, Dhubab, Bab al-Mandab, and Mayyun Island -the Houthis, officially called Ansar Allah, have gained significant leverage over one of the world's vital maritime chokepoints connecting the Red Sea, the Gulf of Aden, and the Suez Canal. Yet al-Shuaibi views Bab al-Mandab as an intermediate objective rather than the final goal. “If the Houthis manage to consolidate their presence in Mocha and Bab al-Mandab, they will gain massive strategic leverage against Saudi Arabia, the United States, and international powers,” he stated. Beyond local military control, al-Shuaibi noted that the move attempts to establish a new regional balance of power, as the Houthis recognize the strait's global economic and political weight. “The more capable they become of threatening the strait, the more enabled they are to transform Yemen from an internal battleground into an influential player in global energy security and trade,” he explained. Netanyahu's 'eighth front': Israel's billion-dollar war on the truth is failing Submitted by Sahar Huneidi on Tue, 09/08/2026 - 17:59 Israel has killed record numbers of journalists and spent more than $1bn on influence campaigns - yet the world has never believed it less People attend a vigil organised by Palestinian journalists to commemorate their killed colleagues at the Nasser Medical Complex in Khan Yunis, in the southern Gaza Strip, on 25 August 2026 (Bashar Taleb/AFP) Off In May 2025, the voice of 14-year-old Hassan Ayyad fell silent. The young Palestinian singer, who captured the world's attention singing "Bear Witness, O World" amid the rubble of the Nuseirat camp, was killed in an air strike . His videos initially went viral, but the reality of the 21st-century information war is that voices like Hassan's are routinely flattened. The systematic silencing of independent war journalism did not happen overnight. It is the result of a 50-year campaign by militaries, governments and now tech monopolies to control what we see - and what we don't. The Vietnam war (1955-1975) was the golden age of independent war journalism. Reporters had remarkable freedom: they could access military transports, follow soldiers on missions and even detach from military escorts. That independence produced graphic, negative coverage that measurably eroded public support for the war. Military commanders blamed what the television critic Michael Arlen had dubbed the "living-room war", the belief that journalistic depictions of bloodshed had created public aversion to conflict. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); The Pentagon learned its lesson. When the US invaded Grenada in 1983, it banned press coverage entirely. Then came the 1991 Gulf war, which became the template for modern information control. Military jargon like "surgical strikes" and "collateral damage" seeped into reporting unconsciously, and the public largely accepted the official story without question. The 2003 American invasion of Iraq institutionalised the "embed" system. Reporters were assigned to military units in exchange for access, but at the cost of independence, with restrictions on where journalists could go, who they could speak with and what they could cover. It is the result of a 50-year campaign by militaries, governments and now tech monopolies to control what we see - and what we don't Independent "unilateral" journalists found themselves unable to get near the action, and a post-war analysis led by Cardiff University found the system left them at far greater risk. By 2007, blogs and social media had begun to break the corporate media monopoly. War blogs from inside besieged Iraq offered raw, unfiltered perspectives, while public trust in American media plummeted from 72 percent in 1976 to 28 percent today. The establishment's grip on war narratives was slipping. But this digital freedom was about to face a counter-offensive of its own. The active complicity of mainstream networks - a phenomenon I have examined elsewhere in the case of Axios - demonstrates that corporate news remains the baseline template for modern information control. Killing the witnesses On 11 May 2022, Shireen Abu Akleh, a prominent Al Jazeera journalist, was shot in the head by an Israeli soldier while covering a raid on the Jenin refugee camp in the occupied West Bank, wearing a vest clearly marked "Press". An investigative documentary later identified the shooter as Alon Scagio of the elite Duvdevan unit. He faced no legal consequences and was instead made a sniper team commander in another special operations unit, before being killed in June 2024 by explosives planted by Palestinian fighters in Jenin - the same city where he had killed Abu Akleh. Her killing fit a pattern the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) had already documented , with at least 20 journalists killed by Israeli military fire between 2001 and 2022 and no one ever held accountable. The war on Gaza has since become the deadliest period for journalism in modern history. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); More than 250 Palestinian journalists and media workers have been killed since October 2023, and CPJ's latest report found 2025 was the deadliest year for journalists on record, with Israel responsible for two-thirds of the deaths worldwide. Israel has also completely barred foreign journalists from independently entering Gaza - an unprecedented step for a state that calls itself democratic. Only controlled military tours are permitted, which participating journalists have described as "theatre". Amid genocide in Gaza, why must Palestinian journalists uphold the illusion of neutrality? Read More » The Foreign Press Association says there are " no security justifications " for the blanket ban, which critics argue serves to maintain a space for denial, allowing Israel to dismiss reports from Palestinian journalists as impossible to verify independently. Israel's obsession with controlling the narrative has its origins in a single defining moment. Those of us old enough remember it vividly. On 30 September 2000, French television captured 12-year-old Muhammad al-Durrah cowering behind his father as bullets struck him during a firefight at the Netzarim junction in Gaza. The 59 seconds of footage aired around the world, and the boy's death became the defining symbol of the Second Intifada. Israel's immediate response was catastrophic for its image: an army spokesman accepted responsibility, assuming Israeli fire had killed the boy. Years later, Israel tried to reverse course, claiming al-Durrah had likely been killed by Palestinian fire, but it was far too late. The narrative was cemented, with Israeli officials later regarding the al-Durrah case as one of Israel's greatest hasbara failures. The lesson drawn was intense and permanent: occupy the information space immediately with a counter-narrative, even if the facts are unverified. When Abu Akleh was killed in 2022, the army's response was immediate and defensive, releasing a counter-narrative within an hour. The al-Durrah incident marked the moment Israel concluded that controlling the narrative - not the truth - was the key to winning the information war. The eighth front Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has explicitly called social media the " eighth front " of Israel's war, alongside the physical battlefields stretching from Gaza to Iran and much in between. He has admitted Israel is losing the propaganda war, attributing the deterioration of support for Israel to the "geometric rise of social media" and the ability of users to share unfiltered imagery from Gaza. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Recognition was followed by a historic financial commitment. The budget of Israel's hasbara machine skyrocketed from approximately $7.5m annually to $150m in 2025, and then to $730m in 2026 - nearly 100 times pre-war levels. Total spending on influence campaigns since 2023 has surpassed $1bn . Epstein files: Western media must stop burying the Israel connection Mohamad Elmasry Read More » A central pillar of this is the "Digital Iron Dome", a platform that describes itself as "the world's first pro-Israel influence engine". It invites users worldwide to join a " digital army ", registering to receive pre-written posts, hashtags and visual content optimised for sharing. The platform claims to have delivered more than 200 million targeted ads across the websites of Al Jazeera, CNN, the BBC, the Guardian and others, and to have reached more than 200,000 websites. Israel also hired Clock Tower X, the firm of Donald Trump's former campaign manager Brad Parscale, on contracts worth $46.5m , in part to shape chatbot outputs and search results by seeding pro-Israel content into the data on which AI models are trained. And under the $900,000 "Esther Project", Israel paid 14 to 18 American influencers, none of whom were registered as foreign agents, between $6,143 and $7,372 per post between June and November 2025. And here, the irony is total. If Netanyahu's strategic planners were looking for a biblical blueprint for asymmetric information warfare, they chose the wrong matriarch. They named their operation after Esther, invoking a queen who hid her identity in a foreign palace. But the true biblical archetype for espionage, safe houses and state-level betrayal belongs to Rahab - the prostitute of Jericho who hid foreign spies on her roof and bought her family's survival with a scarlet cord. Israel's digital architecture operates on the same mercenary transaction, paying actors to manipulate the gates of information from the shadows - an ecosystem of enforced invisibility stretching all the way to Epstein's island . Weaponised algorithms Israel's campaign extends into the platforms themselves. The forced restructuring of TikTok's US operations under Oracle - co-founded by Larry Ellison, a staunch supporter of Israel - was described by Netanyahu as potentially " consequential " for Israel and the Jewish people. Shortly afterwards, TikTok hired Erica Mindel, a former Israeli army instructor, as its new hate speech manager. Leaked data indicates Meta has complied with roughly 94 percent of the Israeli government's takedown requests, removing more than 90,000 pro-Palestinian or critical posts. The playing field was already tilted. Internal documents revealed that Meta lowered the certainty threshold at which its algorithms remove hostile Arabic content from 80 percent to 40 percent for the Middle East - and to just 25 percent for content from Palestine. Israel's campaigns exploited this algorithmic inequality, knowing Palestinian content would be flagged and suppressed long before it could challenge the official narrative. As if this massive PR machinery were not enough, political scientist Ian Lustick and investigative journalist Eli Clifton document a parallel domestic front in their 2026 book Israel's Lobby: America in the Grip of a Foreign Power , showing how the erosion of campaign finance laws has empowered a network of elite donors to manipulate legislative policy and systematically silence dissent. The strategy is clear: kill the journalists, ban the foreign media, co-opt the embeds, weaponise the algorithms and fill the vacuum with curated propaganda. The combination of physical targeting, an embed system that trades access for compliance, corporate consolidation of legacy media, a billion-dollar influence machine and Big Tech's algorithmic bias has created a world in which we no longer see war with our own eyes. We see what the system wants us to see - a staggering reversal, given that the genocide in Gaza was livestreamed in real time by its own victims, who turned smartphones into instruments of unmediated witness. Limits of propaganda For all the billions spent, the influencers recruited and the algorithms weaponised - none of it has worked. The Pew Research Center found this spring that 60 percent of US adults hold an unfavourable view of Israel. Gallup reported in February that, for the first time in a quarter century of polling, more Americans sympathise with Palestinians (41 percent) than with Israelis (36 percent). The numbers in Europe are even more stark. Across six western European countries, between 63 and 70 percent hold an unfavourable view, while in Germany - a nation whose post-war identity is deeply tied to supporting Israel - 73 percent now view the country unfavourably. Among the crucial 18-34 demographic, negative opinions soar to 74 percent in the US and 78 percent in the UK. The Digital Iron Dome has become a monument to the limits of propaganda. No amount of algorithmic manipulation can erase the visual evidence coming from Gaza, the testimony of journalists risking their lives or the growing global moral consensus that what is happening is wrong. What the world has seen during the genocide in Gaza cannot be unseen, no matter how tightly the digital filters are squeezed. We will not simply live in a world of lies; we will live in a world where the truth is no longer available to us - and we will not even realise it is gone Netanyahu's eighth front has not won the war for public opinion; it has lost it and, in doing so, has alienated an entire generation. The silence may have been imposed on social media, but the world is still watching. And the world has made up its mind. We must demand transparency from platforms about their moderation algorithms. We must support independent journalists and the organisations that protect them. We must expose the Digital Iron Dome and the billion-dollar influence industry behind it. And without accountability for murdered journalists, this pattern will repeat itself in Gaza, in Lebanon , in Iran and everywhere power seeks to operate in darkness. I was able to write this piece because I could still ask an AI questions about things I did not fully understand - and receive verifiable answers I could cross-check, question and build an argument from. That freedom is not guaranteed. The same forces that silenced the journalists and captured the platforms are now turning to AI itself. This is the terrifying reality of LLM poisoning: states deliberately polluting the digital ecosystem with curated propaganda, forcing future AI models to absorb lies as objective truth until the authentic record is permanently erased. If they succeed, the next time I ask about Gaza, about Iran, about the warships in the Gulf, AI may not show me the evidence. It may show me a carefully crafted answer designed to protect power - and I will never know what I was not shown. I will not even know to ask a different question. That is the final stage of control: not censorship, but the illusion of information. We will not simply live in a world of lies; we will live in a world where the truth is no longer available to us - and we will not even realise it is gone. The voice of Hassan Ayyad was silenced in an instant. The digital erasure that follows is the sound of democracy dying. This is how truth dies in the 21st century.
