Inflation, again. WITH petrol and diesel prices rising at a steady clip , households are bracing for another round of caustic price increases that burn into monthly budgets and force further belt-tightening. The Sensitive Price Indicator , the weekly inflation gauge published by the Pakistan Bureau of Statistics, was up 8.62pc for the week ended Sept 10 compared to a year ago. Onions, a staple in the local cuisine, had more than doubled in price. Fuel was sharply up: LPG 55pc dearer, and diesel and petrol costing 45pc and 39pc more, respectively, than a year ago. Wheat, another staple, was up 30pc from last year; electricity bills were higher by 25pc. Beef, mutton and chillies were also up by double digits. It bears putting these numbers into perspective: the SPI is deliberately weighted towards tracking daily-use essentials that matter most to lower- and lower-middle-income households. In other words, these numbers represent the cost-of-living squeeze on ordinary Pakistanis. Wages for the vast majority do not keep pace with inflation, which means ordinary people must adjust the only way they can: by reducing usage and consumption. As it is, the inflationary storm unleashed on Pakistan from 2022 onwards has set the vast majority years back in terms of quality of life. Recent statistics show that people are eating less than they did to make ends meet, which is in itself a startling indication of how badly the last bout of prolonged inflation affected households across the country. There has been demand destruction at immense scale, and the local economy may struggle for years to escape this trap. The recent price pressures appear to be driven by the unending war in the Persian Gulf , which has roiled global markets for months now and affected Pakistan particularly intensely due to the country’s dependency on Gulf markets for its energy needs. And there is no indication it will end soon. It is unfortunate that the government has yet to confront the challenge publicly, or show more than a cursory concern for the hardships of ordinary citizens. Granted global oil prices are not in its control, but there are other things it can do. Though the topic now seems taboo, it can still cut the petroleum levy to give relief; all it needs to do is fund the revenue shortfall from another means. It can squeeze undertaxed sectors that have traditionally enjoyed broad exemptions due to political reasons. Authorities must also monitor the produce markets closely and step in to prevent hoarding and profiteering when needed. Inflation has a steep political cost, and lack of visible action will hurt the government in more ways than one. Silence cannot be a policy: at the very least, the citizenry needs an acknowledgment of the challenges they face and a plan to mitigate them. Published in Dawn, September 14th, 2026

Political disconnect. THE disconnect between the government and public concerns could not be starker. While people worry about their economic situation the government is focused on altering the country’s provincial structure. According to the latest Ipsos poll , three in four people believe the country is headed in the wrong direction. The economy and especially inflation are their top concerns. A majority of respondents also said they do not view the economy as strong. It is this low public confidence and pessimism about the future that should concern the government rather than seeking to redraw the provincial map for ill-defined objectives. So far it hasn’t offered any coherent rationale for carving out more provinces. It has also not conducted any study on an issue of such consequence. Although speculation had long been rife about the hybrid government’s intentions it was Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi who made a public pitch for new provinces in July . Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal went further, calling for 15 additional provinces. Each province, he said, should be subdivided into three. As an alternative, he proposed 160 district governments. He argued that establishing more administrative units would deliver effective governance and better social outcomes. The proposal provoked a furious response from the ruling party’s ally, PPP, which opposed any plan to divide Sindh. The party got the Sindh Assembly to adopt a resolution rejecting the division of the province or creation of new administrative units. The MQM, which has long wanted Karachi as a separate province, boycotted the session. It said its proposals were not incorporated in the resolution, including establishing new administrative units. The resolution declared “Sindh is one and shall remain one” and “unequivocally rejected any proposal, plan, scheme or constitutional arrangement … which sought to divide Sindh … or create any new province out of its territory”. Technical fixes are no panacea that will miraculously solve the country’s problems. The government’s attempt to start a debate seemed to flounder and spin out of control after its key coalition partner came out in strong opposition. A senior PPP leader questioned Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s silence and asked him to state his position publicly. Another PPP leader accused federal ministers pushing for new provinces of having a “fake mandate”. Meanwhile, PML-N ministers themselves issued contradictory statements. Rather than clarifying matters, this compounded the confusion and exposed divisions within the party. Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz is also said to be opposed to any division of her province. The joint parliamentary opposition comprising PTI, JUI-F and other smaller parties rejected any plan to divide provinces at its inaugural meeting in late August. Earlier, JUI-F chief Maulana Fazlur Rahman argued this was not the time to divide provinces given the country’s troubled economic and security situation. PTI is now planning a multiparty conference of the opposition on the issue. The party itself has yet to enunciate a clear public position. In the past, it advocated creating a new province in south Punjab. Some PTI leaders say the party opposes changes under “an illegitimate and fraudulent set-up”. The party chairman, however, has urged consultations and said any hasty decision would “harm the federation”. Meanwhile, the leader of the National Party in Balochistan has said creating new provinces would only exacerbate present tensions. None of this has deterred federal ministers from continuing to insist on administrative restructuring. Mohsin Naqvi declared this was essential and no one can stop it. But he added it will only happen with the “will of the people”. He wasn’t walking back from his proposal. His statement implied a referendum might be held to ascertain the ‘will of the people’. Such a move would be deeply controversial and divisive. It would also lack credibility given the history of dubious referendums conducted by past military governments. Questions have also been raised about whether a referendum can constitutionally be used to create new provinces. Proponents of ‘reform’ in the hybrid government ignore the fact that their proposal has already divided the country. It is clear that there is no political consensus on the issue. Consensus cannot be manufactured or coerced. While the government has rammed controversial constitutional amendments and other laws through parliament, using the same method to reorder the provincial structure carries much greater risks. Given the far-reaching consequences of the change and the opposition it faces across the country, the implications would be serious. If pursued, it would further undermine national cohesion and deepen polarisation. There is a clear constitutional procedure to change provincial boundaries. A referendum cannot override that. Any change requires two steps. First a resolution passed by a two-thirds majority in the relevant provincial assembly. Second a constitutional amendment adopted by a two-thirds majority in both the National Assembly and Senate. This effectively gives affected provinces a veto over any change. This requirement cannot be bypassed. Any political manoeuvre to circumvent this will be a disaster. There is no doubt that the governance system needs to be improved. Government should be brought closer to the people to ensure their voices are heard and for better service delivery. But this goal can be realised by empowering local government. It is the third tier of government that needs to be strengthened through functional local bodies as mandated by the Constitution. Improving governance requires more than a technical fix. Above all, it demands an environment grounded in the rule of law. It needs accountability of both leaders and institutions. Administrative changes cannot substitute for competent leadership — with a clear vision and sense of purpose — who are legitimately elected. Good governance also requires prudent policies and much-needed economic reforms shaped and overseen by capable professionals. This is not an argument against administrative change. It is an effort to emphasise three points. First, drawing new provincial lines is not a panacea that will miraculously solve the country’s problems. As noted above, other aspects of governance matter far more. Map-drawing and not fixing fundamentals is meaningless. Second, such changes do not figure among the public’s governance concerns, which are very different. Ignoring those priorities and focusing just on technical fixes will only show how out of touch the government is with people. Third, without broad national consensus, imposing administrative changes will make a mockery of democracy and serve to divide the country. The writer is a former ambassador to the US, UK and UN. Published in Dawn, September 14th, 2026

Extraction and delivery. AS the debate on changing provincial boundaries and decentralisation rages on, it is worth taking a step back to see what is at stake here. What are the main problems that require attention and which have made several people, including entrenched insiders, declare that the current system is ‘broken’ ? The biggest issue being sidestepped by everyone involved (except opposition parties) remains constitutional rule and legitimacy of the state. The current discourse chooses to ignore this, considering it either taboo or a foregone conclusion. Bringing it up seems particularly futile in this discussion given how little it bears on those making decisions and increasingly with those tasked with interrogating these decisions. The second issue is macroeconomic growth, or the absence thereof. What changes are needed to the form of the state that can help kickstart broad-based and sustained capital accumulation? What needs to be done to make the state fiscally more viable? The third issue is social development, and the slowdown in improvement of basic education, health, and other human capability-related indicators. What strategy or approach will help break through the current plateau, marked by a slowdown in literacy rate improvement, a persistently large number of out-of-school children, poor learning outcomes, and no considerable progress on health indicators? When the interior minister talks about a system collapse, the primary subject of this collapse is the state. The Pakistani state, like every other modern state, is engaged in a variety of tasks, none of which it seems to be doing too well. Broadly these tasks can be clubbed under two domains — extraction (getting something from its population) and delivery (doing something for or to the population). There is a third domain — regulation (setting boundaries or implementing rules for various things that private actors may be doing) — as well but we’ll keep that to one side for now. There is no one-size-fits-all approach for the many developmental challenges confronting Pakistan today. The historical record on extraction and delivery is generally poor. Extracting taxes from anyone other than a captive population has proven to be a challenge. Regulating private behaviour, from polluting emissions to urban sprawl to inter-gender interactions, has been difficult as well. And delivering basic services — law and order, education, health — remains highly uneven across rural-urban and provincial lines. If one thinks about the state as the core of a governing system, the track record so far provides ample grounds for a complete overhaul. But a key question to ask is: do all of these functions require an overhaul of the same type? It is possible to look at the exceedingly few examples of success on part of the state in each domain as a blueprint of sorts for what works, especially when thinking about administrative changes. What type of extraction has the state done well and where has it failed? In recent years, the state has done a ‘good’ job of getting people to pay for expensive electricity at cost, rather than delay tariff revisions or provide blanket subsidies. This is an example of a reform that is not really productivity enhancing, but it is certainly something that the state was not doing a decade and a half ago. Similarly, the state has been successful at extracting more taxes from the formal sector and the salaried segment of the population in recent years. This is both by raising the tax rate and by making it ever difficult for the formal sector to avoid its share through an entrenched withholding tax regime. This has happened even while the state has failed to bring many sections of the population into the tax net. When we review the evidence on what enables some types of extraction over others, the absence of discretion and fragmentation of functions comes out as a possible factor. In the case of electricity bills and withholding taxes, the state has centralised collection and removed discretion from its own functions. Local state functionaries have some leeway, sure, but by and large people have no option but to comply and pay directly to the state. In contrast, where economic activity has to be documented by state functionaries themselves (ie, a situation of increased discretion) local politics and influence come into play. On the other hand, the evidence on delivery points in the opposite direction. The biggest gains in social development took place during times of greater decentralisation. When schools were being managed at the school council/local level, improvements in literacy rates and enrolment happened at a faster rate. Similarly, greater autonomy for basic health units and hospitals (with requisite oversight) allowed them to respond to actual patient-level challenges more effectively. Even in delivering basic municipal infrastructure — sanitation and sewage, roadworks — decentralised decision-making and expenditure (between 2002-2008) proved to be more effective. Since province-level centralisation took hold in 2011, gains in key delivery areas of health and education have slowed down. In some parts of the country, outcomes have stagnated altogether. The challenge of delivering to hard-to-access populations has become far more acute. Given this admittedly speculative review of patterns in both extraction and delivery, it is clear there is no one-size-fits-all approach for the many developmental challenges confronting Pakistan today. In domains of extraction, there is an urgent need to reduce discretion and fragmentation of state authority, perhaps even with the use of automated structures in whatever form. In delivery related domains, we likely need even more discretion and fragmentation of the state, via substantive decentralisation that devolves decision-making and accountability down to the level where delivery is supposed to take place. Mangrove cutting for land reclamation at Karachi's Korangi Creek threatens environment. An illegal dyke has been constructed in the heart of a mangrove forest in Korangi Creek, disrupting the natural flow of water and depriving the mangroves on one side of the creek of their essential water supply. As the mangroves dry out and die, they are subsequently cut down by those involved in this illegal reclamation for the sake of land grabbing.—Waqas Ali Ranjha • Forest dept says illegal activity is taking place on its land, but police refuse to act on ‘sub judice matter’ • Experts warn continued loss of mangrove cover could leave Karachi’s coastal areas more vulnerable to natural hazards KARACHI: While cutting mangroves for firewood is a common occurrence, encroachers are active in Karachi’s coastal areas, illegally uprooting mangroves to reclaim land, even next to a biodiversity park at Korangi Creek. The Sindh Forest Department (SFD) confirmed that the illegal activity was being carried out on its land. However, it said police had refused to take action, claiming that the land in question had been allotted by the Board of Revenue and that the matter was sub judice. Dawn visited the Korangi Creek area and found mangrove cutting and land reclamation taking place alongside the Mangrove Biodiversity Park that was inaugurated by Karachi Mayor Murtaza Wahab in September last year. Right beside the erected boundary walls, a large portion of land has been enclosed by an earthen bund to restrict the flow of water towards the mangroves, and the mangroves inside the enclosed area have been cut while their stems are clearly visible in the standing water. In some parts of the bund, a wall is also being erected, while debris has been spread over some of the open area in between, due to which the place is taking the shape of an enclosed plot. A security guard has also been deputed by some private owners to guard the land in question. When Dawn approached the SFD in this regard and inquired about the status of the land and the ongoing activity there, the department sent a team to inspect the site. A senior official of the department said after the inspection that the department was aware of the issue. He said that the land in question belongs to the Forest Department and that such “illegal allotments” were made by the Board of Revenue. The Forest Department, he said, has taken action against such activities several times. In the current case too, they had attempted to take action and remove the bunds. However, the matter was taken by the other party to a court and, therefore, the police refused to take any further action. “And unless the legal issue is resolved, we can’t act on our own,” he added. According to the official, the practice had been continuing for several months. He said creating bunds to stop water from reaching the mangroves was one of the techniques being used for a long time. Once the mangroves dried up, he said, the trees could be cut either by local people seeking firewood or by those involved in the encroachment. The official said the department was making efforts within its mandate to protect the mangroves. Mangroves serve as a natural barrier against hazards Climate change experts and conservationists have expressed concern over the matter. Talking to Dawn , Rafiul Haq, a conservationist and climate change expert, said mangrove cutting had been taking place in the said area for some time and that considerable land had already been encroached upon over the past many years. He warned that continued loss of mangrove cover would leave the coastal area more vulnerable to natural hazards, including tsunamis and hurricanes, as mangroves served as a natural barrier. Therefore, he called for an immediate halt to the cutting of mangroves. Mr Haq also said Pakistan had adequate laws relating to climate change and environmental protection, but the major problem was their implementation. Influential people, he alleged, were often able to evade the consequences of violations. Climate change expert Mas­ood Lohar said mangrove cutting was not confined to the area in question and was also taking place at other locations in Kara­chi and along the Indus Delta. He termed the situation “very concerning” and warned that, in the event of a major tsunami or other coastal disaster, areas including Korangi and DHA could face severe flooding if the natural protection provided by mangroves was lost. Environmentalist Tariq Alex­ander Qaiser stressed the need for greater vigilance to protect the city’s remaining mangrove and tree cover. “All existing mangroves need to be protected. They are critical to the health of our city. They and other trees are a primary element in tackling climate change. Karachi cannot afford to lose its remaining green cover,” he told Dawn. “We need to be more vigilant against such things,” he added. Published in Dawn, September 14th, 2026

Afridi alters tour; security tightened in capital, Punjab. • KP CM to visit deceased PTI worker today • Gatherings of five or more banned across Punjab • 23,500 cops sought for Islamabad security ahead of Sept 27 sit-in • Sanaullah warns against violence, terror threat LAHORE/RAWALPINDI: While Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi has hinted at altering his planned Punjab tour following the demise of a PTI worker, the authorities sprang into action on Sunday with the Centre seeking additional police force from provinces and the Punjab government imposing a ban on gatherings until Sept 17, ahead of the opposition party’s planned march on the federal capital . The PTI had earlier announced a 13-city Punjab tour for Mr Afridi for rallying supporters ahead of a “decisive peaceful protest march” on Islamabad on Sept 27. The caravan was scheduled to start from Daud Khel on Monday to reach Faisalabad for an overnight stay after passing through Mianwali City, Wanbachran, Quaidabad, Joharabad, Khushab, Shahpur, Sargodha, Lalian and Chiniot. The caravan was planned to move from Faisalabad towards Lahore, with a brief stop at Sheikhupura. However, the KP CM said he would visit the residence of the deceased party worker in Lahore first. “Tomorrow, I will go to the home of martyred Ishtiaq Ahmad in Lahore, and after that, I will outline the course of action for the Punjab Street Movement right here in Lahore,” he said. Ban on gatherings across Punjab On the other hand, the Punjab home department banned gatherings of five or more people across the province until Sept 17 under Section 144 of criminal procedure code. The order also forbids the carrying or display of weapons in public and prohibits activity deemed to incite unlawful assembly, though it carves out exceptions for weddings, funerals, religious observance and court and government business. Officials justified the clampdown by citing intelligence suggesting terrorist groups might target large public rallies, saying the aim was to safeguard lives and property rather than to suppress dissent. The scale of the security operation extends well beyond Punjab. Under a federal directive, Punjab has been told to supply 15,000 police personnel for Islamabad’s security, with Sindh contributing 8,000 and Balochistan 500 with a combined deployment of 23,500 officers due to be in place by Sept 20. In Rawalpindi, the city’s police chief, Hassan Mushtaq Sukhera, has cancelled leave for all officers until October, barring genuine emergencies. The police also drew up a list of 179 PTI figures, including sitting and former lawmakers. Also, district authorities have issued preventive detention orders against dozens of PTI workers under Section 3 of the Maintenance of Public Order, including 31 in one Punjab notification and a further 14 in Toba Tek Singh. At the same time, Adviser to the Prime Minister on Political Affairs Rana Sanaullah during an interaction with journalists in Lahore, alleged the opposition party was planning to bring “armed supporters” into Islamabad. Afghan medical students urge govt to stop their repatriation. PESHAWAR: Afghan medical students studying in Pakistani colleges have expressed concern over directives from the Pakistan Medical and Dental Council to return to their country and appealed to the government to allow the already enrolled students to complete their degrees, especially female students, who have no prospects of continuing their education back home. “Currently, about 1,000 Afghan students, including 350 girls, have been pursuing education in medical and dental colleges in Pakistan. The PMDC’s notification asking us to return to our country has caused unrest among us, particularly female students,” said Anayatullah Momand, final-year MBBS student at the Khyber Medical College. Mr Momand, spokesperson for Afghan medical students, said an estimated 200 students who have completed their house jobs and are waiting to be enrolled in specialisation programmes were also among those affected. “The government should allow the currently enrolled students to complete their studies and save their future. We don’t object to Pakistan’s policy of barring Afghans from education here, but the old students should be exempted,” he said. Say PMDC has asked about 1,000 students to return to their home country “Our immense concern is female students who, if sent back to Afghanistan, will sit in homes because there is no education for women due to the Taliban ban,” he said. “All of us had valid visas, and many of the students whose visas had expired have applied for renewal,” he said. According to him, all Afghans have been admitted to colleges on merit. “Some have arrived in Pakistan on scholarship, while others on Afghan national seats reserved by the Pakistan government, and still others are studying under the Pakistan Technical Assistance Programme for Afghans.” “In a recent meeting, the Afghan ambassador to Pakistan told us that they will give us admission in Afghanistan’s medical and dental colleges in case of our repatriation, but we don’t need Afghan medical degrees, which aren’t recognised internationally,” Mr Momand said. “We asked the ambassador what the future will be for female students back home and he had no answer,” he said. “The ball is in the court of Pakistan’s government.” Najma Bibi, a third-year student, said that the danger is not over yet. “Though the Lahore High Court has suspended the PMDC’s directives of July 31 and September 1, which asked the colleges to stop admitting Afghan students, it is a temporary relief,” she said. Bibi, who is one of the 22 students of King Edwards Medical University, which ordered the Afghan nationals to vacate the campus on Sept 7, said the PMDC should take pity on hundreds of Afghans, especially female students, and reconsider its decision. “The decision aims to send us to the Stone Age because the Taliban in Afghanistan have banned women’s education,” said another student on condition of anonymity. A 3rd-year MBBS student, she came to Pakistan two years ago on the Allama Iqbal Scholarship offered by Pakistan, with the hope to complete her education and serve women back home. “However, these past few months have been like hell, and we still face the risk of eviction from Pakistan,” she said. A first-year female student said that her dream of becoming a doctor is unlikely to get materialised given the threats they are facing. “Pakistan should realise our problem, as going back can land us in a hard and challenging situation and even we can face prosecution,” she said. On Sept 1, PMDC had asked the medical and dental colleges that enrolled Afghan students to return to Afghanistan, in accordance with the prevailing policy directions. The institutions concerned shall ensure that necessary administrative formalities, including issuance of the requisite No-Objection Certificate and facilitation of their departure, are completed accordingly, the directive said. Security forces kill 3 terrorists, including commander, in Balochistan's Mastung: state media. Security forces have killed three terrorists during an operation in Balochistan’s Mastung, state media reported on Monday, citing security sources. The troops targeted a vehicle of Fitna-al-Hindustan — a term the state has designated for Balochistan-based groups to highlight India’s alleged role in terrorism and destabilisation across Pakistan — using a quadcopter during the operation, APP and Radio Pakistan reported. The precision strike killed three terrorists, including a commander, while the vehicle was completely destroyed, the reports said. Balochistan has witnessed an increase in terrorist attacks in recent weeks, prompting security forces to intensify counter-terrorism operations. Last month, the number of terrorist attacks in the province increased by seven per cent from 83 in July to 89 in August, according to a monthly assessment by the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies. On the night of Aug 31-Sept 1, terrorists of the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) launched a coordinated attack on the Customs House, located at Ziarat Cross on the N-50 National Highway, in the Pishin district. In retaliatory action, security forces killed 10 terrorists while two officers were among six martyred in the fire exchange, according to the military’s media affairs wing. Also on Aug 31, 11 terrorists belonging to Fitna-al-Hindustan, who had blocked the N-40 Quetta-Taftan highway by establishing an illegal checkpoint for extortion in Chagai’s Nokcha area, were killed following an intense exchange of fire. On Sept 2, security forces killed 12 terrorists in the Kalat district during an intelligence-based operation (IBO). Days later, the troops killed 11 terrorists and recovered 2.9 tonnes of explosives during separate IBOs in Kharan and Washuk districts. Another 36 terrorists were eliminated during multiple “high-tempo” operations conducted in Mastung, Quetta, Kalat and Sibi districts, the Inter-Services Public Relations said on September 4. These also included thwarting an attack on a police station in Sibi’s Bhag area.

PPP’s Attaullah Shah edges past IPP's Imam Malik after counting of postal ballots for Diamer seat. GILGIT: PPP’s Attaullah Shah was declared the winner for the GBA-16 (Diamer-II) seat in the Gilgit-Baltistan Assembly on Monday following the completion of verification and counting of postal ballot papers. Final consolidated results detailed in the Form-49 released by the GB Election Commission showed that Shah garnered 6618 votes, beating the first runner-up, Istehkam-i-Pakistan Party’s (IPP) Imam Malik, by 13 votes. Malik had contested the June elections in GB as an independent candidate, but had later joined the IPP. Initially, the Election Commission had declared him the returned candidate for GBA-16 (Diamer-II), but his membership was suspended last week after Shah filed a petition before an election tribunal. The plea contended that the returning officer (RO) had issued Form-49 without counting the postal ballots. In its order on September 11, the tribunal directed the relevant RO to complete the verification and counting of postal ballot papers by September 16 and, meanwhile, suspended Malik’s membership. Subsequently, the counting and verification of postal ballots for GBA-16 (Diamer-II) commenced amid tight security on Sunday. The RO had directed all contesting candidates to ensure their presence in the proceedings, either in person or through their authorised representatives. But, Malik and PML-N’s Muhammad Anwar did not appear either in person or through an agent, according to a statement issued by the Election Commission. It said that the proceedings on postal ballots were started under Section 235 of the Election Act, 2017, in the absence of the candidates or their representatives. PPP’s Khan and other candidates, Mohammad Nasir and Saifullah, were represented by their agents during the process, that went on for hours. The verification and counting was conducted in the presence of Gilgit Senior Civil Judge Fahad bin Naqeeb, Assistant Registrar of the Chief Court Raj Mir and Deputy Election Commissioner Muha­mmad Ali. Malik’s supporters remained outside the Election Commission Secretariat throughout the night as the counting continued. Later, a large number of PPP supporters also gathered outside the secretariat to celebrate Shah’s victory, distributing sweets and shouting party slogans. The dispute over the seat had earlier triggered protests by supporters of both candidates in Diamer, with PPP workers blocking the Karakoram Highway and Malik’s supporters staging a sit-in outside the Returning Officer’s office. The dispute dates back to the June elections, when Malik was initially declared the winner. Shah later challenged the result, arguing that postal ballots had not been counted before Form-49 was prepared, leading to the tribunal’s order for their verification and counting. Meanwhile, the Gilgit-Baltistan Supreme Appellate Court is scheduled to hear Malik’s appeal against the election tribunal’s decision to suspended his membership today (Monday). Islamuddin Advocate, Shah’s counsel, had earlier told Dawn that Justice Sardar Muhammad Shamim Khan will decide whether the case is admissible or not.

Indian government pushes wider rollout of polarising civil code. India’s interior minister has vowed to further implement a contentious common civil code for states governed by the ruling Hindu nationalist party, a move expected to stoke concern among minority Muslims. India’s 1.4 billion people are subject to a common criminal law, but rules on personal matters such as marriage, divorce and inheritance vary based on the customary traditions of different communities and faiths. The introduction of a Uniform Civil Code (UCC) to replace those diverse rules has been a long-standing goal of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). At least four states have implemented the UCC so far. “We have introduced the UCC in several states … I am confident that we will implement (it) in all 21 states governed by the BJP-led National Democratic Alliance by 2029,” Home Minister Amit Shah said on Sunday. The campaign for a standardised civil code has raised concerns, especially among Muslim citizens, who say such a move would infringe on their religious freedoms. Supporters say the UCC gives Muslim women the same rights as others by ending polygamy, setting equal property inheritance rights for sons and daughters, and requiring divorce processes to take place before a civil court. India, the world’s most populous country, is majority Hindu. It is also home to an estimated 220 million Muslims, giving it the world’s third-largest Muslim population. India’s next national elections are due in 2029, after Modi won a third successive term in 2024, when he was forced into a coalition government.

'India started a war based on a lie and lost miserably': Bilawal reacts to Indian media's attempt to link Pakistan to terrorism. PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari on Monday reacted to Indian media’s attempts to link Pakistan to terrorism, saying that the neighbouring country had “started a war based on a lie and lost miserably”, a reference to last year’s May conflict. Bilawal made the remarks on the social media platform X, while reacting to Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s interview with an Indian media channel. In an interview with NDTV , Ibrahim — who was in India to attend the BRICS summit over the weekend — was asked if he considered Israel’s actions against Hamas terrorism. “Yes, it is terrorism,” Ibrahim replied. The host then asked if “by that token”, what “Pakistan has done against India and in Pahalgam” would be considered “terrorism”. “I would not go to that extent. I know it is very sensitive to say that in India. I’m a close friend of Modi ji , and we engage with the Pakistanis,” the Malaysian prime minister said. Asked why the Malaysian PM was “not as direct in criticising Pakistan for terrorism”, Ibrahim said: “Well, it has to be established.” He continued: “I mean, none of my intelligence establishment … would come back and tell me, ‘Anwar, yes, there was state-sponsored terrorism’. Therefore, I, as the prime minister of Malaysia, would then refer to this fact.” Reacting to the clip of the interview, Bilawal said on Monday: “Malaysian PM exposing Indian propaganda, in India on Indian TV. The truth is India started a war based on a lie and lost miserably.” He said that India now stood “exposed internationally”. “India must live up to its commitments made at the time of the ceasefire; to discuss all friction points with Pakistan. So we can together bring peace, prosperity and stability to our region,” he said. In May 2025, a four-day conflict between Pakistan and India was sparked by an attack on tourists in occupied Kashmir’s Pahalgam, which New Delhi, without evidence, linked to Pakistan. Islamabad strongly denied responsibility while calling for a neutral investigation . After New Delhi launched deadly air strikes in Punjab and Azad Kashmir on May 7, Pakistan said it downed five Indian planes in air-to-air combat, later raising the tally to eight . After tit-for-tat strikes on each other’s airbases, it took American intervention on May 10 for both sides to finally reach a ceasefire . In April, on the first anniversary of the Pahalgam attack, Pakistan had rejected a renewed Indian propaganda campaign linking it to the attack, deploring that the neighbouring country was focusing on “weaponising its false narrative” in the midst of a regional crisis sparked by the US-Israel war on Iran.

FCC says jail manual 'clear' on transfer of prisoners to hospital. ISLAMABAD: The Federal Constitutional Court (FCC) on Monday questioned the validity of the jail manual if it was to be applied discriminatorily, adding that it was “clear” on the transfer of prisoners to hospital. The court made the observations while hearing pleas filed by inmates at Adiala jail seeking treatment at private hospitals, similar to the relief granted to PTI founder Imran Khan. The inmates had moved the Islamabad High Court (IHC) last month seeking relief after the Supreme Court (SC) on August 18 directed the authorities to transfer Imran to Shifa International Hospital for medical examination and treatment. However, the petitions were dismissed on August 31 after IHC held that a prisoner had no legal right to be transferred to a private hospital of his choice and the primary responsibility for prisoners’ treatment rested with the state’s administrative structure and government hospitals. Subsequently, the inmates approached the FCC last week to challenge the IHC order. A three-member FCC bench headed by FCC Chief Justice Aminuddin Khan, including Justice Ali Baqar Najafi and Justice Aamer Farooq, took up the petitions on Monday. Advocate Akhtar Cheena appeared on behalf of one of the prisoners, Muhammad Ilyas Khan, while the other inmates — Mohammad Ismail Hussain and Owais Altaf — were represented by Advocates Irfan Nasir Cheema and Syed Jaffer Baqir, respectively. “There should not be any discrimination when the jail manual is very clear,” observed Justice Najafi during the hearing. “Why only private hospitals for treatment and not hospitals like the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (Pims) or the Poly Clinic Hospital when Rule 197 of the Pakistan Prison Rules 1978 is very clear?” asked Justice Farooq. Rule 197 of the Pakistan Prison Rules, 1978 governs the manner and mode of the transfer of a prisoner, the expense of which has to be borne by the state. During Monday’s hearing, when advocate Cheena cited the SC’s Aug 18 order, CJ Khan asked why the lawyer had not chosen to become a party in the case regarding Imran’s transfer to a private facility pending before the SC, which is scheduled to be heard on Sept 16. The lawyer, however, responded that the present appeal was filed under Article 175E of the Constitution against the IHC order. Under Article 175E, the FCC has exclusive original jurisdiction in disputes between the federal and provincial governments. However, its powers will be limited to issuing declaratory judgments rather than enforcing decisions directly. The counsel said that relief similar to that granted to Imran had become necessary after the Aug 18 order. The FCC postponed further proceedings to Sept 15 (Tuesday), observing that the case involved interpretation of the law. One of the inmates’ appeals had contended that Rule 197 prescribed that prisoners could be shifted to a civil hospital, arguing that the distinction being drawn by the government that the term only referred to a public hospital was wrong. The petition said the wording implied a distinction between a military and government hospital, adding that against the backdrop of the Aug 18 SC order, any inmate with a serious ailment could be shifted to a private hospital for treatment, paid by their family. The petition said the client had severe internal bleeding issues and had been brought to the public hospital for treatment eight times during the last two months. “Given the condition of the public hospital system, we have no trust that my client will get appropriate medical attention at a public hospital,” the petition said.

KARACHI AND THE LONG SHADOW OF 9/11. For Raja Umer Khattab, Karachi changed before the city fully understood what was happening. Moving to the Sindh Police’s specialised unit in early 2002 — later named the Counter Terrorism Department (CTD) — the veteran police officer was deeply familiar with Karachi’s typical violence: primarily deadly sectarian conflicts that seldom utilised explosives. But the threat rising in the shadow of 9/11, 25 years ago, was unlike anything Khattab and his colleagues had ever faced. As American firepower ousted the Taliban’s first regime and shattered the Al Qaeda network in Afghanistan, the war spilled across the border. It didn’t stop in Pakistan’s rugged tribal belt; it flowed south into the sprawling, chaotic metropolis of Karachi — quietly at first and then with devastating force. The city was becoming something its law enforcement agencies had never been trained to confront: a staging ground for “a transnational jihadist war”, says Khattab, a highly decorated officer who recently retired after spending the bulk of his 35-year police career on the CTD frontlines. While Pakistan’s tribal areas offered sanctuary, Karachi offered reach. Highways connected the port city and the country’s business hub to the rest of the country and its international airport linked to the wider world. Its vast population provided anonymity, while established networks of jihadi groups and madressahs [religious seminaries] supplied contacts, funding, logistics and recruits. A quarter of a century after the infamous events of September 11, 2001, which launched America’s so-called ‘War on Terror’, Zia Ur Rehman looks back at how those events transformed militancy in Pakistan in general and the city of Karachi in particular. Drawing on his own reporting over two decades and the experiences of recently retired Raja Umer Khattab, one of the frontline police officers involved in counter-terrorism operations, he assesses how the terror landscape has changed in these 25 years… Then came the attacks. In January 2002, Wall Street Journal reporter Daniel Pearl was kidnapped and subsequently murdered. In May 2002, a suicide bomber targeted a bus carrying French naval engineers outside the Sheraton Hotel. The next month, the US Consulate was struck . Christian institutions came under attack. Other incidents followed in rapid succession. Investigators immediately spotted the fingerprints of displaced Al Qaeda operatives fusing with local factions. “We realised almost immediately that this was completely different from the violence we knew,” Khattab recalls. “We had to adapt fast, leveraging the deep human intelligence we’d cultivated over years on the sectarian frontlines.” That distinction would define the next two decades. Karachi became a place where global jihadist networks, Pakistani militant organisations, sectarian groups, violent political actors and criminal networks intersected — sometimes cooperating, sometimes competing and often becoming difficult to distinguish from one another. Khattab lists one militant organisation after another that had operated in Karachi: “Al Qaeda, Jundullah, Lashkar-i-Jhangvi [LJ], Sipah-i-Muhammad Pakistan [SMP], Harkat-ul-Mujahideen Al-Alami, the Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan [TTP], Ansarul Sharia, Baqiatullah, Al Qaeda in the Indian Subcontinent [AQIS], Islamic State Khorasan Province [SKP], the Zainabiyoun Brigade, Jamaat-ul-Ahrar…” He pauses and admits that he can no longer remember the names of all the groups he had dealt with over the years. Banned Baloch and Sindhi ethno-separatist groups, including the Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) and the Sindhudesh Revolutionary Army, added another layer to the city’s already volatile militant landscape. The important story, however, is not simply that militant groups operated in Karachi. It is how the nature of that militancy changed after 9/11. By 2009, the TTP’s presence had begun to transform Karachi’s militant landscape. The militants displaced from tribal areas by Pakistani military operations did not simply seek refuge in the city. They increasingly established themselves in its urban periphery, particularly in Pakhtun-majority neighbourhoods. Raja Umer Khattab describes the period from 2008 to 2014 as one of “absolute devastation” for Pakistan and Karachi. THE FIRST DRAGNET The city soon became the frontline of a high-stakes international manhunt. Hadi Kakar, a Quetta tea stall owner, remembers September 2002 with vivid clarity. A large number of uniformed police and plainclothes intelligence operatives suddenly converged on Karachi’s Defence area, surrounding a three-story building near his shop. “Heavy gunfire broke out for hours, but we were completely in the dark,” Kakar recalls. “When police officers stopped by for tea later, they mentioned some Arab militants had been arrested.” The raid unfolded on the first anniversary of 9/11. The primary target was Ramzi Abdullah bin al-Shibh, a key Yemeni operative who later acknowledged his role as a central planner of the 9/11 attacks. His capture was part of a sweeping dragnet triggered by Pakistan’s entry into the US-led ‘War on Terror.’ Working alongside America’s Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Pakistani security forces spent those early months tracking Al Qaeda operatives who had fled the collapse of the Taliban regime in Afghanistan. While many believed this influx was a sudden post-9/11 retreat, Al Qaeda’s roots in Karachi ran deep, long before 2001. In 1998, Mohammed Sadiq Odeh, a key player in the US Embassy bombings in East Africa, was arrested at Karachi Airport. Abu Ahmed al-Kuwaiti, Osama bin Laden’s trusted courier, also operated a safe house in the city during those formative years. Post-9/11 operations merely brought these existing ties into the light. The crackdown on Al Qaeda further escalated after Gen Pervez Musharraf narrowly escaped two assassination attempts in Rawalpindi within two weeks in December 2003. A fierce backlash followed. A group of young militants, radicalised under the influence of two physician brothers accused of having links with Al Qaeda, Arshad Waheed and Akmal Waheed, forged ties with Al Qaeda and formed Jundullah, a group distinct from the Iranian organisation of the same name. It went on to carry out a series of high-profile attacks, including a 2004 attempt on the life of Karachi’s then corps commander . One of the brothers was killed in a US drone strike in South Waziristan in 2009 and was later eulogised by Al Qaeda in its publications. Over the next few years, joint intelligence operations systematically dismantled the upper ranks of the Al Qaeda network. High-profile Al Qaeda figures, including Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, Abu Zubaydah, Abu Faraj al-Libi, Mustafa al-Hawsawi, Ahmed Khalfan Ghailani, Naeem Noor Khan and Yonis al-Mauritani were hunted down across the country. Karachi itself yielded crucial captures, including Hassan bin Attash, Ammar al-Baluchi and Walid bin Attash. Yet, the more the senior leadership was hunted, it also exposed Karachi’s role not just as a refuge but as an urban laboratory, where foreign jihadist doctrine integrated with local networks. Simultaneously, Khattab recalls, the city endured brutal tit-for-tat sectarian violence, driven by groups such as LJ and SMP, marked by mass casualty attacks — such as the 2006 Nishtar Park rally bombing that decimated the top Barelvi leadership and the 2009 Ashura procession bombing. THE ARRIVAL OF THE TTP By the late 2000s, the threat was changing again. My own journalism and research career began in the shadow of that shifting war, around the time Al Qaeda was strategically bringing disparate Taliban factions operating across the border districts together under the TTP banner in 2007. By 2009, the TTP’s presence had begun to transform Karachi’s militant landscape. The militants displaced from tribal areas by Pakistani military operations did not simply seek refuge in the city. They increasingly established themselves in its urban periphery, particularly in Pakhtun-majority neighbourhoods. Khattab describes the period from 2008 to 2014 as one of “absolute devastation” for Pakistan and Karachi. I covered this transformation in Karachi extensively from the ground. Police officers were hunted in broad daylight along their patrol routes. Militants established control over parts of the city’s peripheral localities, running extortion networks, imposing their own rudimentary forms of justice and targeting polio vaccination teams, educationists and political activists, particularly those associated with the Awami National Party (ANP). The TTP presence in Karachi was itself fragmented mainly due to the abundance of easy extortion revenue. Factions were organised largely along regional lines, reflecting where militants had originated, including Swat, South Waziristan and Mohmand. These semi-autonomous groups controlled their own areas and revenue streams. During this period, the TTP’s central chief, Mufti Noor Wali, also served as the group’s Karachi chief. To consolidate their position, TTP factions forged alliances with local jihadist and sectarian groups, particularly the LJ. The TTP could bring manpower, weapons and suicide bombers. Local militants brought something equally valuable: knowledge of Karachi. “Born, raised or deeply embedded in Karachi, these local operatives understood the city’s complex urban geography,” Khattab says. The cooperation eventually developed into operational coordination involving the TTP, Al Qaeda and foreign militant groups, such as the Islamic Movement of Uzbekistan. Together, they mounted sophisticated attacks on high-value military targets, including the 2011 assault on the Pak Navy base PNS Mehran and the June 2014 attack on the Jinnah International Airport in Karachi . The airport attack proved to be a major turning point. It triggered Operation Zarb-i-Azb in the tribal areas — crippling the TTP and other Al Qaeda-affiliated militant groups over the following years — while accelerating Karachi’s security crackdown, launched in September 2013. Led by the paramilitary Rangers and supported by the CTD, law enforcement forces systematically dismantled the TTP networks that had taken root across the city. In his book Inqilab-i-Mehsud , TTP chief Noor Wali acknowledged that the crackdown severely weakened the group’s Karachi operations and led to the deaths of several senior commanders. FROM ORGANISATIONS TO NETWORKS By the middle of the 2010s, another change was taking place. As foreign Al Qaeda operatives moved towards the Afghan border, or were killed or captured through raids, the organisation’s influence did not simply disappear. It left behind local recruits, splinter factions and ideological sympathisers capable of sustaining militant activity in new forms. In 2014, Al Qaeda leader Ayman al-Zawahiri attempted to formalise these loose elements by establishing AQIS, appointing Asim Umar as its leader — a figure already known locally for his popular conspiracy books on Islamic eschatology and the Dajjal. According to Khattab, AQIS relied heavily on existing networks in Karachi, absorbing local factions to build its operational core. A key faction was Harkat-ul-Mujahideen al-Alami, which had split from the mainly Kashmir-focused Harkat-ul-Mujahideen (HuM) during the early 2000s. HuM al-Alami had orchestrated several high-profile attacks in Karachi, including the 2002 assault on French engineers and the 2004 bomb blast near a concert featuring Indian singer Sonu Nigam. While AQIS signalled its ambitions through high-profile actions, such as the attempted 2014 hijacking of a Pakistani Navy frigate , its true impact was structural rather than tactical. Unlike foreign fighters, local operatives possessed deep knowledge of the urban terrain, allowing them to blend seamlessly into the city. Investigations into individual attacks routinely exposed complex, interconnected networks rather than isolated cells. “An investigation into a single bombing would lead to a completely different organisation or cell,” Khattab explains. Instead of operating in isolation, militant factions built fluid alliances, borrowing personnel, tactics and specialised expertise. The declaration of the Islamic State (IS) caliphate in Iraq and Syria introduced a competing model of jihadism. Frustrated by Al Qaeda’s perceived caution, some disgruntled TTP leaders, including Daud Mehsud (a TTP militant and a former Karachi policeman), shifted their allegiance to IS. Yet, Khattab maintains that IS never succeeded in establishing a permanent, structured presence in Karachi. Muhammad Israr Madani, an Islamabad-based researcher on militant ideologies, notes that Pakistan’s jihadist landscape has long been dominated by Deobandi groups, leaving little breathing room for IS’s aggressive Salafism to build a recruitment base. He explains, “Even though Al Qaeda was also Salafi-leaning, it chose not to emphasize its Salafi identity when dealing with local Deobandi groups in the Pakistan-Afghanistan region.” But the significance of this period lay less in which organisation gained the upper hand than in how militancy itself was changing. The old, hierarchical structures were giving way to looser networks, in which people, money, skills and ideology could move across organisational lines. THE MILITANT NEXT DOOR The most unsettling sign of this transformation was that the militant no longer had to come from the borderlands. He could come from Karachi itself. When I asked Khattab which single event had most shaken the city’s intelligence apparatus, his answer was immediate: the May 2015 massacre in Safoora Goth , when gunmen boarded a bus and killed 45 members of the Ismaili community. “The pressure on us was immense,” Khattab recalls. For law-enforcement agencies, the attack represented more than another episode of violence. It exposed a fundamental change in the profile of the militant. These were not simply hardened fighters arriving from remote border areas. Khattab says, “We were facing a new kind of militant — educated, urban, professionally employed and socially integrated, who had embraced jihadist ideology while continuing to live within ordinary social environments.” I had seen signs of that shift myself. I knew university students involved in Islamist campus groups and urban militant networks, such as Hizb ut-Tahrir, who became radicalised, eventually gravitating towards Al Qaeda and other militant factions. Some eventually left Karachi for Afghanistan and the tribal areas, where they took up arms and were killed. High-profile cases, such as the one of Saad Aziz, an elite business school graduate, and Noreen Leghari, a medical student, exposed a troubling trend of self-radicalised, educated youth, forcing authorities to look more closely at how educated young people were being drawn into militant groups. At a 2017 conference I attended, senior CTD officials, such as Omar Shahid Hamid, consulted academics, security experts and civil society to build a targeted counter-narrative against campus recruitment. The Safoora Goth massacre was perhaps the clearest expression of that transformation. The cell behind it, which also killed prominent activist Sabeen Mahmud and targeted several police officers, comprised educated, locally rooted operatives. They maintained operational ties to Al Qaeda while attempting to align themselves with the IS’s rising global brand. According to Khattab, the subsequent crackdown effectively prevented IS from establishing a sustained presence in Karachi. By 2017, the CTD had also dismantled Ansarul Sharia, a shadowy group composed largely of middle-class, highly educated, young men who targeted security personnel. The pattern was now unmistakable. The large hierarchical organisations had broken down into concealed, highly localised and self-organising cells. A US official examines the wreckage of a van after a powerful vehicle bomb exploded outside the US consulate building in Karachi on June 14, 2002: such incidents followed in rapid succession in 2002 as Karachi became a city where global jihadist networks, Pakistani militant organisations, sectarian groups, violent political actors and criminal networks intersected | AFP GLOBAL JIHAD AFTER THE WAR ON TERROR A quarter-century after 9/11, the global terrorscape forged by the so-called ‘War on Terror’ has evolved into something quieter and far more elusive. The US has long withdrawn its forces from Afghanistan and the Taliban have returned to power. Years of relentless counterterrorism campaigns, drone strikes, high-profile leadership losses and organisational fragmentation have undeniably weakened Al Qaeda, while its primary rival, IS, has also weathered significant operational setbacks. Yet, a question remains for regional and international security analysts: has Al Qaeda drifted into permanent irrelevance, or has it simply learned to adapt? “There are two schools of thought,” argues a diplomat working for a Western mission in Islamabad who studies militant organisations in the region. “Some say Al Qaeda is a spent force, irrelevant to the modern jihadist landscape, while others believe its current position reflects strategic silence and that it will return.” There are reasons for both interpretations. The US response to 9/11 battered Al Qaeda, decimating its senior leadership, destroying its safe havens and severely crippling its capacity to launch large-scale global operations. Yet, such experiences also force jihadi organisations to evolve. The rise and fall of the IS provided a stark lesson. Its attempt to establish and govern a self-declared caliphate brought it into direct confrontation with a vast international military coalition and demonstrated the enormous cost of openly holding territory. For Al Qaeda and its affiliates, long-term survival meant shifting away from territorial governance toward cultivating local ties, preserving clandestine networks and wielding quiet ideological influence. Meanwhile, the geopolitical landscape around them changed too. Former Al Qaeda allies — such as the Taliban in Afghanistan and Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham (HTS) in Syria — went from being the world’s most wanted terrorist groups to running governments. This didn’t mean the movement was dying. Instead, it showed that these groups had learned a crucial lesson: surviving and keeping power matters more than pulling off dramatic attacks. THE QUIET NETWORKS Nowhere is this tactical shift more alarming than along the volatile Pakistan-Afghanistan border. Following the Taliban’s takeover of Kabul in August 2021, Pakistan’s two border provinces, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan, were hit by a sharp revival of violence. The Taliban’s success in Afghanistan handed local groups such as the TTP a surge of momentum, ideological validation and safe havens across the border. This cross-border support threatens to erase the hard-won security gains achieved through costly military campaigns, such as Operation Zarb-i-Azb. Behind this increase in militant activity is a pattern of quiet cooperation. Intelligence reports suggest that the AQIS has closely linked itself with local militant groups, especially the TTP, following the 2022 killing of Zawahiri in Kabul by a US drone strike, an incident that highlighted the Taliban’s breach of the Doha agreement. This arrangement allows Al Qaeda to maintain its regional influence while helping protect the Taliban regime in Kabul from pressure by Islamabad, Beijing and Western governments, which are demanding action against foreign militants operating from Afghan territory. A recent UN Security Council report highlighted how closely these groups are now connected. It said that Al Qaeda’s official media house, As-Sahab, issued an explicit endorsement of TTP strikes against Pakistani state assets. More importantly, the report said that the AQIS now functions as the “operational backbone” of Ittihad-ul-Mujahideen Pakistan, an umbrella group led by Hafiz Gul Bahadur, the militant originally from North-Waziristan responsible for some of the deadliest suicide attacks against security forces. EVOLVING SHADOW OVER KARACHI To the casual observer, Karachi today feels transformed. Unlike the border provinces of KP and Balochistan, currently enduring a relentless surge of armed violence, Karachi has largely been spared the constant, high-intensity terrorism that defined its recent past. During its bloodiest years, the metropolis was gripped by daily targeted assassinations, sectarian violence and brazen assaults on strategic installations. The decisive security operation launched in September 2013 effectively shattered the entrenched infrastructure that allowed armed factions to control entire neighbourhoods. That calm, however, is deceptively fragile. In 2023, a heavily armed TTP assault team breached the Karachi Police headquarters, triggering an hours-long siege in the heart of the city. More recently, militants from Jamaatul Ahrar, which recently splintered from the TTP, targeted a Sindh Rangers facility. In a media briefing, senior CTD officer Irfan Bahadur explained how such cross-border attacks depend on hidden local cells. An arrested facilitator and his network provided intelligence, carried out reconnaissance in the city and arranged safe passage for four militants who travelled directly from Afghanistan to attack Karachi. This reveals the primary takeaway from Karachi’s security history: militant groups function as fluid, adaptive networks rather than rigid structures. A Karachi-based madressah teacher with past links to jihadist circles explains, “Leaders are killed. Factions splinter. Names are erased or changed, and loyalties trade hands. But personal relationships and extremist ideologies survive every crackdown.” Detained in 2008 by legendary CTD officer Chaudhry Aslam, who was killed by a TTP suicide bomber in 2014, the teacher was cleared and later aided law enforcers in navigating the city’s jihadi underworld. He stresses that human intelligence, not brute force alone, is crucial to dismantling the older militant groups. “CTD officers such as late Aslam, Khattab, Bahadur and Hamid spent years building deep informant networks across the city’s jihadi landscape,” he says. “Now that many of those officers are dead, retired or reassigned, some of that institutional memory may have been lost.” He adds a warning: “The new generation of police officers, many with limited understanding of Karachi’s militant underworld, could face a daunting task if a fresh militant wave strikes.” This fluid dynamic is precisely what confronted Khattab and other law enforcers after 9/11. It became glaringly obvious during the TTP’s urban expansion and grew even harder to trace as groups adapted into micro-cells linked to Al Qaeda and IS. That frontline duty exacted a heavy toll. Khattab and his family survived two separate assassination attempts over his career. A quarter-century after the first American bombs fell in Afghanistan, the original ‘War on Terror’ may have ended. However, the underlying ideology and informal networks remain intact. “We won’t see a simple repeat of the post-9/11 years,” Khattab notes, pointing to decades of counter-terrorism operations that dismantled Karachi’s old militant ecosystem — its facilitators, safe houses, funding channels and legacy jihadi groups. Yet, the threat has simply adapted, transitioning from visible command structures into elusive, decentralised cells. Countering it requires mapping the underlying connective tissue before it ignites again. “These cells need only a spark,” Khattab warns. “They have simply shifted into the shadows, waiting for the right moment to re-emerge.” The writer is a journalist and researcher whose work examines the intersections of militancy, political violence, faith, migration and rights across Pakistan.
