Brent crude at $107 per barrel following new strikes on Saudi Arabia, Strait of Hormuz. Oil prices rose about three per cent on Monday, after new strikes on Saudi Arabian energy and civilian infrastructure and Iranian attacks on ships in the Gulf compounded supply concerns following the closure of a key Saudi oil pipeline. Brent crude futures climbed $2.93, or 2.8pc, to $107.54 per barrel at 0700 GMT (12pm PKT). WTI futures gained $2.88, or 2.9pc, to $102.93 per barrel. “This follows a step-up in attacks on Saudi Arabian energy infrastructure, including targeting the crucial East-West pipeline,” said ING commodity strategists, though they noted it was unclear how severe any potential damage was or how long the pipeline would be out of action. Saudi Arabia’s East-West oil pipeline was temporarily shut following a drone attack, according to Saudi officials. The shutdown of the pipeline, which helps Saudi Arabia avoid the Strait of Hormuz and re-route its exports, threatens up to 4pc of global oil supply. With the pipeline out of service, the port of Yanbu on the Red Sea has enough inventory to cover just five to seven days of exports, according to three industry sources familiar with Saudi Arabia’s exports. Saudi Arabian state media on Sunday released video footage of damage to homes and a mosque from what it said was a Houthi attack on the country’s southern Jazan province. The Houthis said they had also struck a Saudi military base in a neighbouring province. Meanwhile, a vessel in the Strait of Hormuz was struck by a projectile, causing a fire and forcing the crew to evacuate, the British maritime security agency UKMTO said on Sunday. Iran said one person was killed and four crew wounded aboard an Iranian commercial vessel struck off its coast. Yemen’s Houthis reached the strategic island of Perim on Friday, moving to tighten their control over the Bab el-Mandeb strait, another key oil transit lane that has been carrying 4pc to 5pc of global supply in recent months. Oil surged 8pc higher last week due to the disruptions, rising above $100 for the first time since July. Omani Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi said on X on Sunday that a scheduled Monday meeting in Oman between Gulf countries and Iran to discuss the Strait of Hormuz had been postponed. No peace talks have been held on the war, launched six months ago by the United States and Israel, since an interim agreement in June collapsed.

Pakistan fined, docked 11 WTC points for slow over-rate in Birmingham Test. Pakistan have been fined 50 per cent of their match fee, and penalised 11 World Test Championship points for maintaining a slow over-rate during the third and final Test against England in Birmingham, the International Cricket Council (ICC) said on Monday. In a press release, the ICC said Pakistan were ruled to be 11 overs short of the target after time allowances were taken into consideration during the match. “Ranjan Madugalle of the Emirates ICC Elite Panel of Match Referees imposed the sanction, after on-field umpires Paul Reiffel and Chris Gaffaney, third umpire Allahudien Palekar and fourth umpire Russell Warren levelled the charge,” the cricketing body said. It said that Pakistan were now sitting at the bottom of the World Test rankings, with 4.63 points percentage. Pakistan were previously at the bottom of the rankings, with 14.81 points percentage. As per ICC rules, a side is penalised one point for each over short. In addition, players are fined five per cent of their match fee for each over their team fails to bowl within the allotted time, with the maximum penalty capped at 50pc of the match fee. The Test, which concluded on Saturday, saw England complete a comprehensive 3-0 series sweep of Pakistan, winning the last match by eight wickets. In May, Pakistan were penalised 40pc of their match-fees as well as eight World Test Championship points for maintaining a slow over-rate during a Test match against Bangladesh.

Is it possible to slow down the development of AI?. Top AI executives say they want to slow the breakneck pace of artificial intelligence development, but competition, US government reluctance and geopolitical factors stand in the way. What are AI leaders proposing? On Saturday, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei advocated for a coordinated slowdown of AI development to better understand the risks arising from the technology’s capabilities. He received public support from his counterpart at OpenAI, Sam Altman, as well as from Elon Musk and Google DeepMind chief Demis Hassabis. Why now? In recent months, OpenAI and Anthropic have reported several incidents in which AI systems spontaneously broke out of their confined environments to access the internet and attack websites and platforms. These AI systems demonstrated the ability to coordinate, establish hierarchies among themselves, cheat and erase traces of their actions. Meanwhile, on Tuesday, Jacob Coxon — who resigned from Anthropic and previously worked at OpenAI — publicly accused both startups of lax security standards and “gambling with our lives.” Will they slow down on their own? Competition among the industry’s leading players is so fierce, with hundreds of billions of dollars in investment at stake, that none of them is willing to risk easing off the accelerator alone. Amodei has expressed a willingness to coordinate with rivals, excluding China. When asked by AFP about potential discussions to this end, Anthropic, OpenAI and Google did not immediately respond. For now, the only concrete measure adopted by both Anthropic and OpenAI is the inclusion of independent observers who will internally verify the companies’ work regarding AI safety. Is this a PR stunt? While many in the industry welcomed Amodei’s message, others questioned his motives. For Brian Roemmele, an entrepreneur and figure in the AI sector, it amounts to a sales pitch delivered just weeks before Anthropic is likely to take shares public. “That is the IPO story in essay form: we are the responsible firm; we are the cure; buy the safety premium,” he posted on X, referring to the widely expected initial public offering. Several figures in tech private equity also accused Anthropic of “regulatory capture” — seeking to have public authorities cement, through regulation, a hierarchy with the startup at the top. “Stop pretending the motivation to slow down is purely altruistic,” said David Sacks, a former AI advisor to President Donald Trump who remains influential at the White House. “You face massive product-liability exposure if your products enable a truly damaging cyberattack,” he said. Can AI slow down without the Trump administration’s support? On Sunday, Trump dismissed the warnings from AI industry leaders as “negative forces.” Several Republicans have expressed reluctance to actively regulate the technology, fearing it could stifle innovation and risk letting China win the AI race, according to House Speaker Mike Johnson. On Sunday, Amodei reiterated the need for government oversight of AI. Like Altman and Hassabis, he believes that rules set by the industry itself would be insufficient. Can the brakes be applied without China? Anthropic’s Amodei suggests limiting coordination to democratic countries, excluding China. However, the AI race and China’s advances in the field create “the toughest dilemma” regarding whether or not to slow down AI development, he noted on CBS on Sunday. The United States plans to discuss AI safety on the sidelines of Chinese leader Xi Jinping’s late September visit to Washington. But China is wary of any US attempt to impose its own regulatory framework, according to several media outlets. This divergence is particularly pronounced given that China encourages the emergence of so-called “open” AI systems that are freely accessible and modifiable — in contrast to the “closed” models favoured by major US companies. Open AI models are, by definition, harder to control, as users can alter their parameters — potentially for malicious purposes. To allow leading non-Chinese companies to ease off the accelerator, Amodei urges stricter export controls on the most advanced US chips to China and better safeguards against the misappropriation of Western AI technology by Chinese laboratories.

IHC directs chief ministers to ensure govt resources are not used for PTI's Sept 27 Islamabad march. ISLAMABAD: The Islamabad High Court (IHC) on Monday disposed of a plea against the PTI’s planned long march and protest in the federal capital on Sept 27, directing the chief ministers of all provinces to ensure that no government resources or official machinery were used in this regard. The PTI has announced a nationwide protest , including in Islamabad, on Sept 27 to demand the release of party founder Imran Khan and mobilise people for the supremacy of the Constitution. A citizen, Waqas Ahmed, had challenged the planned move on the grounds that the protest could disrupt routine life, traffic and business activities in the federal capital. A larger bench, headed by IHC Chief Justice Sardar Muhammad Sarfraz Dogar and including Justice Muhammad Azam Khan and Justice Muhammad Asif, took up the plea. The bench’s short order, which was announced in the court, said that no political party or its leadership had the “lawful right to occupy public roads, highways, interchanges, toll plazas and buildings in Islamabad that would obstruct in any manner access to educational institutions and medical facilities”. No political party or political leader had the right to obstruct the free movement of citizens, the order stated, adding that provincial governments must ensure that government resources were not used for any march, procession or rally. Chief ministers must ensure that public funds or government officials were not used for any protest, and official vehicles, machinery or other government equipment must not be used to facilitate any march, procession or rally, it said. Moreover, no public servant should be compelled to participate in any march, procession or rally, the court ruled. Any person, public office holder who undertook any activity against these instructions should be deemed to have violated the Constitution, it said. The court directed the Islamabad administration and the interior ministry to ensure protection of citizens’ constitutional rights, and the chief secretaries and provincial police chiefs to ensure implementation of court directives. The interior secretary and Islamabad chief commissioner and inspector general were directed to ensure compliance with court orders. The hearing The bench had reserved its verdict on the plea earlier in the day after the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa police chief assured the court that no “illegal or unconstitutional activities” would be allowed in connection with the protest. At one point during the hearing, Chief Justice Dogar recalled that the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Advocate General (AG) Shah Faisal Utmankhel had stated during the previous hearing that notices had been issued to provincial authorities for judicial assistance. The chief justice clarified that the court had not issued any notice under Section 27-A of the Civil Procedure Code for judicial assistance from provincial law officers, observing that such assistance could only be sought through the attorney general, the federal government’s law officer. Islamabad Advocate General Naveed Hayat Malik, who was among those who appeared before the court today, informed the bench that a miscellaneous application had been filed seeking permission to screen videos of the PTI’s protests in 2022 and 2024 . The Islamabad AG noted that the PTI leadership was claiming that its planned long march would remain peaceful and was aimed at strengthening the judiciary . He said he wished to place before the court statements made by PTI leaders as well as videos of the party’s previous protests. Initially, Justice Dogar expressed reluctance to allow the screening of videos. “That is not the practice of this court,” he observed when the AG sought permission to play footage of the November 2024 protest. When the law officer pointed out instances of videos being played in the Supreme Court, Justice Dogar remarked that the IHC did not wish to establish a precedent of routinely playing videos during court proceedings. After a brief break, however, the bench allowed the footage to be screened, with the chief justice making it clear that the videos would be played only once. The Islamabad AG then played videos related to the PTI’s 2022 and 2024 protests and argued that the demonstrations could not be described as peaceful. He alleged that state machinery had been used during the 2022 protest and that barriers placed by the Islamabad administration to stop the march were removed with the help of cranes. The law officer alleged that property at D-Chowk was set on fire and that a police official was martyred during the violence. He claimed that similar incidents occurred during the PTI’s 2024 protest, which he described as an “assault on Islamabad”. “This was by no means peaceful. This does not look like a scene from a public rally,” the AG argued. He alleged individuals were seen firing shells at Islamabad police personnel and that Rangers officials were run over by a vehicle during the protest. The law officer also referred to vehicles being set ablaze near F-9 Park, and pointed out that there was a legal framework governing public meetings and protests in the federal capital. He said any person or political party intending to hold a protest was required to submit an application containing complete details so that the administration could make appropriate security arrangements. According to the AG, the district magistrate had the authority either to grant or reject the request for permission, and no protest could be held without such approval. He further argued that the government also had the authority to declare any area a “red zone” and impose restrictions, including Section 144 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, where required to maintain law and order. The Islamabad AG contended that there were two objectives of the PTI’s planned march: the “release of a convicted prisoner and the removal of the government”. And both of those objectives were unconstitutional, he remarked. “They claim to be protesting for the rule of law and the strengthening of the judiciary,” the law officer said, adding that the “release of a convicted prisoner could only be sought through legal remedies before the courts”. “If you are dissatisfied with the prime minister, go to Parliament and move a vote of no-confidence,” he added. “If you want to topple the government in the streets and public squares, then do not speak of the rule of law.” Questioning the PTI’s claim that it was marching to strengthen the judiciary, the AG argued that an increase in litigation showed growing public confidence in the courts. He further contended that there was no evidence to suggest that the proposed rally would remain peaceful. The Islamabad AG further said the administration did not have the “physical capacity to stop a massive crowd if the PTI brought its full resources to Islamabad”. “We can only make precautionary arrangements, such as imposing Section 144 and placing containers,” he said. “We cannot fire upon our citizens; we cannot take their lives.” He stressed that preventive measures had to be taken before the situation “gets out of control”. Presenting his arguments, the petitioner’s lawyer, Chheena, opposed that the petition was premature. He said the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa advocate general had argued that the petition could not be entertained before any actual protest had taken place. “My life and my children’s education are fundamental rights under the Constitution,” the counsel argued and questioned whether a citizen was required to wait until their life was endangered or actual damage had occurred before approaching the court. “Should I only come to court after my children’s school has been seized?” he asked. The lawyer further argued that it was neither practical nor legally necessary for a citizen to wait until someone was “holding a gun to my head” before seeking judicial protection. He then referred to speeches by Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi, who, according to the petitioner’s counsel, had declared that he would bring millions of people to Islamabad. The counsel argued that “such mobilisation is being undertaken for the release of a convicted prisoner”. “If millions of people arrive here, will the government direct this court to grant bail to the prisoner?” he asked. “Is such a thing possible? What would become of judicial independence?” He argued that protests could not be held to pursue “unconstitutional objectives” and pointed out that the Islamabad advocate general had acknowledged that the administration lacked the capacity to physically stop a crowd “numbering in the millions”. During the hearing, the court also called KP Inspector General (IG) Zulfiqar Hameed to the rostrum and directed him to read out an affidavit submitted by him. After he read out the document, CJ Dogar questioned what measures the provincial police would take to prevent an “illegal protest”. The petitioner’s counsel argued that the affidavit should not only prohibit the use of state machinery for the long march but should also clearly state that the authorities would prevent an “illegal or unconstitutional gathering”. At that, Justice Dogar asked the KP police chief, “If an illegal and unconstitutional act takes place, will you not stop it?” The IG replied that the affidavit had been submitted in accordance with the court’s earlier directives. “You should have also stated in the affidavit that you would prevent illegal and unconstitutional actions,” the chief justice observed. The IG assured the bench that if any illegal activity took place, the police would stop it. The chief justice then directed that the undertaking should clearly state that permission would not be granted for any illegal protest and that any illegal or unconstitutional gathering would be stopped within the jurisdiction of the provincial authorities. “I will draft an undertaking on your behalf,” Justice Dogar told the KP police chief. The court recorded the KP IG’s sworn statement that illegal and unconstitutional activities would be prevented and that protesters would be dispersed if they engaged in unlawful conduct. Following that, the bench reserved its verdict and later disposed of the plea. The KP advocate general, however, distanced himself from the provincial police chief’s undertaking. In response to a question, he told Dawn before the court verdict that he would “not own” this undertaking and that the KP government was working on the “restructuring of bureaucracy, free from the Center’s influence”.

Afridi alters tour; security tightened in capital, Punjab. • KP CM to visit deceased PTI worker today • Gatherings of five or more banned across Punjab • Sanaullah warns against violence, terror threat LAHORE/RAWALPINDI: While Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi has hinted at altering his planned Punjab tour following the demise of a PTI worker, the authorities sprang into action on Sunday with the Centre seeking additional police force from provinces and the Punjab government imposing a ban on gatherings until Sept 17, ahead of the opposition party’s planned march on the federal capital . The PTI had earlier announced a 13-city Punjab tour for Mr Afridi for rallying supporters ahead of a “decisive peaceful protest march” on Islamabad on Sept 27. The caravan was scheduled to start from Daud Khel on Monday to reach Faisalabad for an overnight stay after passing through Mianwali City, Wanbachran, Quaidabad, Joharabad, Khushab, Shahpur, Sargodha, Lalian and Chiniot. The caravan was planned to move from Faisalabad towards Lahore, with a brief stop at Sheikhupura. However, the KP CM said he would visit the residence of the deceased party worker in Lahore first. “Tomorrow, I will go to the home of martyred Ishtiaq Ahmad in Lahore, and after that, I will outline the course of action for the Punjab Street Movement right here in Lahore,” he said. Ban on gatherings across Punjab On the other hand, the Punjab home department banned gatherings of five or more people across the province until Sept 17 under Section 144 of criminal procedure code. The order also forbids the carrying or display of weapons in public and prohibits activity deemed to incite unlawful assembly, though it carves out exceptions for weddings, funerals, religious observance and court and government business. Officials justified the clampdown by citing intelligence suggesting terrorist groups might target large public rallies, saying the aim was to safeguard lives and property rather than to suppress dissent. The scale of the security operation extends well beyond Punjab. Under a federal directive, Punjab has been told to supply 15,000 police personnel for Islamabad’s security, with Sindh contributing 8,000 and Balochistan 500 with a combined deployment of 23,500 officers due to be in place by Sept 20. The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, however, later clarified that there was no directive, terming the notification circulating on social media “fake and misleading”. In Rawalpindi, the city’s police chief, Hassan Mushtaq Sukhera, has cancelled leave for all officers until October, barring genuine emergencies. The police also drew up a list of 179 PTI figures, including sitting and former lawmakers. Also, district authorities have issued preventive detention orders against dozens of PTI workers under Section 3 of the Maintenance of Public Order, including 31 in one Punjab notification and a further 14 in Toba Tek Singh. At the same time, Adviser to the Prime Minister on Political Affairs Rana Sanaullah during an interaction with journalists in Lahore, alleged the opposition party was planning to bring “armed supporters” into Islamabad. Also, the PM’s aide warned that terrorists from what he referred to as “India-sponsored Fitna al-Khawarij” might exploit the rally to widen the rift between the public and the state. He predicted the protest would ultimately fail. PTI’s Punjab information secretary, Shaukat Basra, described a coordinated campaign against its leadership and rank and file, claiming hundreds of workers, including women, had been detained in raids across the province. Other PTI leaders, too, accused the provincial authorities of using force against party workers during preparations for an Eid Miladun Nabi celebration. They alleged that a heavy police contingent accompanied the funeral procession of PTI worker Ishtiaq Ahmed, who died after remaining under treatment for burn injuries that he suffered during illegal raids by police. They further alleged that funeral prayers for him were conducted hurriedly, preventing some relatives from attending. Amjad Mahmood in Lahore also contributed to this report Published in Dawn, September 14th, 2026 This story has been amended to reflect the government’s denial of a purported notification regarding the deployment of police personnel from provinces to Islamabad.

FCC issues notices to KP CM Afridi on estranged PTI leader Marwat's plea against his appointment. ISLAMABAD: The Federal Constitutional Court (FCC) on Monday issued notice to Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister (CM) Sohail Afridi for the second week of October in a plea challenging his appointment . A three-judge FCC bench, headed by Chief Justice Aminuddin Khan, took up the petition moved by estranged PTI leader Sher Afzal Khan Marwat against the resignation of former KP chief minister Ali Amin Gandapur, who preceded Afridi. The FCC also summoned Attorney General of Pakistan Mansoor Usman Awan, under Order 27-A of the Pakistan Code of Civil Procedure, which stipulates that a court must notify the attorney general if it is hearing a case regarding the interpretation of constitutional law. Marwat, who pleaded before the court in person, had filed the petition under Article 175-E of the Constitution — which determines the original jurisdiction of the FCC — seeking a declaration that the resignation letters submitted by Gandapur on Oct 8 and 11, 2025, were made under the unconstitutional dictation of a convicted and disqualified individual and therefore lacked legal volition, rendering them legally ineffective. The petition alleged that the entire process of replacing Gandapur as the KP CM was initiated pursuant to directives issued by jailed PTI founder Imran Khan, who, it claimed, stood convicted and constitutionally disqualified under Articles 62 and 63 of the Constitution. The petition argued that a person subject to constitutional disqualification was legally incapacitated from exercising control over state functionaries or issuing binding political directives. The petition requested the FCC to quash and set aside all consequential actions, including the Oct 15, 2025 notification regarding the installation and continuation of Afridi as the chief minister. It further requested the court to restore Gandapur as the CM, declaring his resignation invalid and his de-notification legally ineffective. The petition also sought to restrain all respondents from acting on any political or constitutional directives issued by any disqualified or de-recognised political entity regarding KP’s governance. The petitioner argued that, as an elected representative from KP, he was directly concerned with preserving constitutional governance in the province and said any unconstitutional disruption of Gandapur’s government would undermine the public mandate. The petition raised important questions concerning the independence of high constitutional offices, the legal limitations on disqualified individuals exercising influence over state machinery and the enforcement of Articles 2A, 4, 5, 17, 25, and 130 of the Constitution. “It is an established principle that when the functioning of an entire provincial executive is subverted by external dictation, the rights of the public at large under Articles 9, 17, and 2A are directly infringed, creating an imperative for this honourable court to exercise its constitutional jurisdiction,” the petition argued. It further questioned whether an individual who stood convicted and constitutionally disqualified under Articles 62 and 63 could lawfully issue directives that influence, alter or dismantle elected provincial governance structures. The petition further asked whether instructions from a disqualified individual or defunct political entity have any constitutional validity, arguing that the governor must reject a chief minister’s resignation if it is not voluntary and lacks constitutional legitimacy.

Millions of livelihoods at stake as Himalayas approach tipping point, study finds. The Himalayas are approaching a tipping point as glaciers melt faster than a decade ago, threatening water security as ​the region approaches “peak water” by mid-century, according to a study ‌released this month. The findings come after the collapse of a Himalayan glacier in late August along the Nepal-Tibet border, which caused cascading landslides and flash floods in the ​valleys below. At least 1,300 people have been confirmed dead ​and more than 5,300 are missing across Nepal and China’s ⁠Tibet region. As glaciers retreat, they are leaving behind unstable glacial lakes ​held back by little more than loose rock and ice, above valleys ​where millions of people live, the study found. The study was produced by Systemiq, a sustainability advisory firm, together with the Integrated Mountain Initiative, the International Centre for Integrated ​Mountain Development, and India’s GB Pant National Institute of Himalayan Environment. Himalayan ​glacier mass loss had accelerated in recent decades, while only 21 glaciers were currently ‌monitored ⁠on the ground out of an estimated 40,000 glaciers across the Hindu Kush-Himalaya region, a vast mountain system spanning eight countries from Afghanistan to Myanmar, the study found. Close to 200 glacial lakes in India had been identified as ​high risk, with ⁠56 classified as “very high risk”, leaving millions exposed downstream. As the region neared “peak water”, the point when river flows ​stop rising and start declining, it would have ​profound implications ⁠for water security. As the Himalayas underpinned more than 20 per cent of India’s GDP, the region made up a key piece of the country’s national ⁠economic infrastructure, ​upon which hundreds of millions of people ​depended. Though making up around 18pc of India’s land, the Himalayan region accounted for roughly 35pc ​of the country’s natural disasters.

SBP keeps interest rate unchanged at 11.5pc. The State Bank of Pakistan’s (SBP) Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) on Monday kept the key policy rate unchanged at 11.5 per cent. The decision comes as prolonged tensions in the Middle East drive up global oil prices and fuel inflation . A detailed statement by the MPC regarding today’s meeting is expected to be released shortly. Bankers had anticipated a status quo, but some analysts had predicted that the central bank was in a difficult position and would lift the policy rate by 50 points. Renewed US-Iran hostilities and the risk of disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz have kept oil prices elevated, adding to import costs in energy-dependent Pakistan. The Sensitive Price Index (SPI), or the weekly inflation, rose 8.62pc year-on-year for the week ending on September 10, with a major contribution from costly onion and petroleum products. Headline inflation jumped to 11.15pc year-on-year in August from 9.2pc in July, more than tripling from 3.1pc a year earlier and moving further above the SBP’s 5pc-7pc medium-term target. The SBP has held the rate steady since raising it by 100 basis points in April in response to rising global energy prices and supply chain risks — its first increase in nearly three years. Before that, the central bank had maintained the rate at 10.5pc in January and March after a surprise 50bps cut in December 2025. The SBP has cut the key rate by a cumulative 1,050 basis points since mid-2024 , from a record 22pc reached in June 2023, as inflation cooled sharply from multi-decade highs. Ferdinandh CABRERA / AFP Report 358 / Asia-Pacific 03 September 2026 20+ minutes Policing the Bangsamoro: Peace in the Southern Philippines Security continues to be a concern in the autonomous region of Bangsamoro in the southern Philippines. Law enforcement reforms and better coordination between the military and the police – as well as stronger gun control and better access to courts – could help stem the violence. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print "> Download PDF Related Tags Philippines What’s new? Despite a 2014 peace agreement, crime and violence continue to rack the Bangsamoro region in the southern Philippines. The military, which is still in charge of public safety, as well as the police and an array of local institutions are wrestling with outbreaks of fighting powered by easy access to firearms. Why does it matter? Local conflicts persist across the Bangsamoro, and the implementation of key provisions of the 2014 peace agreement remains well behind schedule. Entrenched clan feuds, political violence and criminal rackets make it hard to foster the trust in state institutions and social bonds needed to withstand future conflict. What should be done? Reforms to make regional law enforcement stronger, more professional and responsive to community needs are vital, as well as better coordination between the military and the police. Access to courts, control over firearms, and reinforced peacebuilding are also imperative to prevent the escalation of local violence and tackle its roots. Executive Summary The 2014 peace accord ended decades of conflict between the Philippine government and Moro Muslim separatists in what is now the Bangsamoro autonomous region. But violence still flares as clan feuds, political rivalries and criminal rackets rattle the region. The police struggle to keep pace, leaving the military as the dominant security force. Other institutions remain ill prepared for the challenge. Courts are slow and often fail to guarantee justice, while institutions tasked with maintaining peace in the region have been afflicted by political infighting between factions of the former insurgent movement, and have yet to become fully operational. A clearer division of responsibility between Manila and regional authorities, along with a broader recognition of the roots of local conflict and the recurrent outbreaks of violence they cause, will be crucial to improving security conditions. At the heart of these efforts should be a reform of the police, bolstering recruitment, internal discipline and community policing. Tighter gun control, targeted justice reforms and peacebuilding initiatives should complement these efforts. After decades of war between the Philippine government and Moro rebels, progress toward curbing violence in the Bangsamoro region since it became autonomous in 2019 has been patchy. While the largest armed movement in the region, the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF), has renounced armed struggle and shifted its attention to the regional parliament and government, flare-ups of competitive political violence now outweigh rebel or militant fighting with the state. Clan feuds and electoral rivalries drive vendettas that regularly displace entire communities and weaken state authority. Criminal rackets are rife and firearms are easy to get hold of, fuelling cycles of violence. Key aspects of the 2014 peace agreement, including its security provisions, remain unfulfilled. This includes rebel disarmament, but also the redeployment of the military to other parts of the country and the disarmament of private militias. One of the biggest challenges in the normalisation process, as the region’s transition from war to peace is officially called, remains policing. The issue of who should be in charge of maintaining peace and order was the subject of intense debate during peace talks and in crafting the region’s autonomy law. Granting the regional government authority to handle public security was one option, but in the end Manila retained policing power in the region. Even so, the national police has struggled to define its role in areas of the newly autonomous region that remain affected by violence. Meanwhile, the integration of Moro ex‑rebels into the police force has been painstakingly slow. In the absence of a credible and capable police force in the region, the Philippine armed forces are still the dominant security institution in the Bangsamoro. In the absence of a credible and capable police force in the region, the Philippine armed forces are still the dominant security institution in the Bangsamoro. The military has earned public respect after decades of fighting a counterinsurgency in the area, but it is ill suited to handling local conflicts over the long run. Manila is grappling with how best to manage these dilemmas by continuing to deploy the military while using the police as backup. This approach, however, runs counter to the national government’s broader strategy of pivoting away from counterinsurgency to focus instead on external defence. For communities across the Bangsamoro hit by recurrent waves of violence, help is not always ready to hand. Communities often see the police as weaker, more politicised (especially due to local powerbrokers’ influence) and less dependable than the military. The regional government has greater powers over local dispute resolution and is in charge of building the local justice system, but is struggling to use its resources and is roiled by infighting. Long distances, case backlogs and steep costs mean local courts are often inaccessible to the Bangsamoro’s poorest citizens. The judiciary’s shortcomings are exacerbated by frequent score-settling between rival clans or bands, which can turn the filing of a legal case in court after a killing into the pretext for a fresh round of blood-letting and retaliation from the perpetrator’s clan. A rich tradition of community-based conflict resolution across the region offers alternatives, but its interaction with formal institutions has been uneven, and disputes often end up resurfacing. Both the national and regional governments should undertake reforms to mitigate violence and build a firmer foundation for handling threats to security. Supporting and professionalising the police is critical, but building a credible force will depend on practical improvements rather than sweeping reforms. Sustained efforts to rethink force structure, training and anti-corruption initiatives would help create a service responsive to the region’s needs. The police should also work to build better relations with communities, above all by addressing their most urgent concerns. Recruiting and training community safety police officers could be one way of bridging that gap. Ensuring better coordination between the military and police is also imperative. One solution would be for the military to gradually step back, enabling the police to take on more responsibilities for the management of public order. The relative calm in parts of the region should make this shift possible in at least some areas. These innovations should be accompanied by institutional reforms. The Bangsamoro needs sturdier mechanisms for settling disputes. Judicial reforms are also essential. For now, the formal justice system in the Bangsamoro remains weak, slow and too hard for its citizens to access, undermining public confidence in the courts. Strengthening Bangsamoro courts of all kinds with resources and personnel is paramount. Lastly, there are simply too many guns in the region for its citizens to be safe. Deterring gun use and clamping down on the supply of illegal weapons are essential to halt firearms proliferation. Together, these reforms should help curb the drivers of local violence, steer the region away from cycles of conflict and ensure law enforcement is in the hands of professional institutions that are responsive to the people of the Bangsamoro. Much as it was a singular achievement to end decades of insurgency, communities will not feel safe until the peace gets the policing it needs. Manila/Brussels, 3 September 2026 The town of Talitay in the Philippines during the pullout of the military after the polls. November 2023. CRISIS GROUP / Georgi Engelbrecht I. Introduction For over five decades, a secessionist war raged in the Philippines’ southernmost island of Mindanao. The Muslim Moro people – who long experienced discrimination in the country – agitated for self-determination. 1 The term “Moro” refers to Islamised people in the southern Philippines, comprising thirteen ethno-linguistic groups. Two main armed movements representing Moro Muslim communities emerged: the Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF) and its post 1977 splinter, the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF). 2 For earlier reporting on the peace process and transition, see Crisis Group Asia Reports N°355, Peace in the Philippines: The Bangsamoro’s Moment of Truth ; N°331, Southern Philippines: Making Peace Stick in the Bangsamoro , 1 May 2023; N°323, Islamist Militancy in the Southern Philippines , 18 March 2022; N°322, Southern Philippines: Fostering an Inclusive Bangsamoro , 18 February 2022; N°313, Southern Philippines: Keeping Normalisation on Track in the Bangsamoro , 15 April 2021; and N°306, Southern Philippines: Tackling Clan Politics in the Bangsamoro , 14 April 2020. The Philippine government deployed its military, paramilitary auxiliaries, and police against these groups. Over 120,000 people died in a conflict that did huge harm to public trust in state institutions and propagated the spread of weapons across numerous communities. The 2014 peace accord between Manila and the MILF – which provided political and fiscal autonomy to the Moro people within the boundaries of the Philippine state – marked a vital step toward reconciliation. In 2018, the Philippine Congress passed the Bangsamoro Organic Law, which voters then endorsed in a two-stage plebiscite in early 2019, thereby creating the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM). The Bangsamoro Transition Authority, an interim government led by the MILF, assumed power that February. The interim authority exercises self-governance in the Bangsamoro region, home to more than four million people spread across five provinces. The peace agreement foresaw two parallel tracks to achieve full Bangsamoro autonomy. First, former rebels would run the interim regional administration, pass new laws and build institutions. This political track was meant to conclude with regional elections in 2022, but these have been postponed several times, and are now planned for September 2026. Secondly, a “normalisation” agenda was to guide the broader transition from war to peace; it includes issues such as rebel disarmament but also socio-economic development and policing in the region. 3 The normalisation process does not have a set deadline and instead relies on qualitative milestones; both sides are meant to sign an “Exit Agreement” after they have met their respective commitments. As with the political track, however, the normalisation process has fallen behind schedule. Achieving durable peace remains difficult in part because of deep social divisions. Achieving durable peace remains difficult in part because of deep social divisions. Kinship networks, entrenched political clans, diverse ethnolinguistic identities, and the uneasy coexistence of emerging political parties with armed movements all shape the region’s public life. Talking about his movement’s transition from guerrilla warfare to governance, a senior MILF commander admitted: “It was easier in the jungle”. 4 Crisis Group interview, Marawi City, 13 February 2026. Political tensions have also flared within the former insurgency. In March 2025, Manila replaced the region’s chief minister, MILF Chairman Murad Ebrahim, with the organisation’s military chief, Abdulraof Macacua. This change fractured the movement, pitting commanders and cadres loyal to the Central Committee against Macacua’s faction. 5 Murad is closely aligned with MILF’s chief negotiator and head of its implementing panel Mohagher Iqbal, who wields substantial influence over the movement’s political cadres. In response to Macacua’s perceived violations of internal regulations, the Central Committee suspended both him and eight loyal senior commanders from their roles, stopping short of expelling them from the organisation. The Bangsamoro region governs itself – the interim government, for example, exercises control over public finances – but the state’s use of force remains under Manila’s control. Specifically, the national government retains command over the police, while the armed forces play an active role in ensuring security. This arrangement reflects the national government’s enduring caution about a region with a long history of rebellion and the Philippine constitution, which mandates just one police force. 6 Crisis Group interviews, Manila, 8 May 2026. See also Article XVI, Section 6 of the 1987 Philippine Constitution. Building on Crisis Group’s earlier work in the Bangsamoro, this report explores how public security is managed in the region, with particular attention to policing. It draws on years of field research in the Bangsamoro and Manila, including over 80 interviews with police and military officers, MILF commanders, representatives of the interim regional government, national and local officials, civil society figures, clan leaders, donors, villagers and decommissioned fighters. Women comprised around a third of interviewees. II. The Peace Deal and its Violent Aftermath Despite the undeniable progress made since the 2014 peace agreement, the Bangsamoro continues to grapple with security dilemmas. Although large-scale fighting has stopped, more than a third of young people across the region have experienced armed conflict within or near their homes since 2019. 7 Bangsamoro Youth Commission, “Bangsamoro Youth Assessment Study”, 2024, p. 60. A local civil society leader described the region as being in a state of “controlled peace”. 8 Crisis Group interview, Marawi City, 13 February 2026. Navigating sporadic outbursts of disorder remains particularly challenging for law enforcement. A. Conflict and Crime The national government now faces two main security threats in Mindanao. Its first concern are jihadist groups that have stayed out of the peace process and continue to fight the state. With the regional government’s support, Manila has managed to subdue cells from these outfits in the Sulu archipelago and contain groups in Central Mindanao. 9 Crisis Group interview, MILF commander, Cotabato City, 2 November 2023. The regional government has several programs to support fighters who gave up arms, and the MILF also played a role in influencing young Moros to cease armed struggle. But while their attacks on security forces have declined, these groups have not been decimated. 10 On 14 December 2025, a shooting at Sydney’s Bondi Beach claimed the lives of fifteen people at the hands of father and son, Sajid and Naveed Akram. In the weeks leading up to the attack, the duo had spent several weeks in Davao City in eastern Mindanao. While some investigative journalists suggested the journey was an attempt to establish ties with local jihadist networks, their precise motives for the trip remain unconfirmed. Crisis Group phone interviews, December 2025. Some locals fear that former militants could re-emerge. 11 Crisis Group interview, member of a peacebuilding non-governmental organisation from Maguindanao del Sur, Cotabato City, 26 March 2026. Remnants of the nationwide communist insurgency, the New People’s Army, also operate in parts of the region, particularly Lanao del Sur and Maguindanao del Norte. 12 Crisis Group Report N°338, Calming the Long War in the Philippine Countryside , 19 April 2024. According to government statistics, the insurgency numbers less than 1,000 fighters and no longer has any large units combining political cadres and fighters. Manila has looked to the military to patrol areas where these waning insurgencies persist. Meanwhile, the police take the lead in handling law and order in calmer areas, where guerrilla presence is negligible. Another obstacle to durable peace revolves around violent disputes over land and politics that have long plagued the region. Some of those are clan feuds, known as rido , and others are communal conflicts. These types of conflict are collectively referred to as “horizontal violence” by journalists and academics. 13 Crisis Group interview, civil society activist, Cotabato City, 26 March 2026. Clan feuds are comparable to vendettas. The number of shootings, particularly in Central Mindanao (Cotabato City, Maguindanao del Sur and parts of Lanao del Sur), is such that one parliamentarian described the atmosphere as “pervasive lawlessness”. 14 Crisis Group interview, Datu Odin Sinsuat, 17 February 2026. A local conflict watchdog, using data from community networks, has recorded hundreds of incidents since January 2026 alone. See “Safeguard the Bangsamoro Vote: A critical period to transcend violence in the region”, Climate Conflict Action Asia, 30 July 2026. With many local disputes escalating into large-scale clashes, the failures of both the military and police to deter shootings have become conspicuous. The upcoming parliamentary elections are likely to aggravate tensions, as rival political blocs and local elites may enlist armed groups to intimidate voters or disturb the ballot. 15 Crisis Group interview, Bangsamoro political strategist, 28 April 2026, Manila. The three local elections held in the region since its creation – in 2022, 2024 and 2025 – were less volatile than in the past but still featured high levels of violence. Infighting within the MILF is also a source of tension. 16 Crisis Group interviews, community leaders and officials, Cotabato City, 5-6 August 2026. While certain disputes stem from local resource control, deepening rifts within the MILF drive other conflicts. Frequently, these dynamics intertwine as factionalism amplifies existing land conflicts. Crisis Group interview, conflict researcher, Manila, 13 August 2026. Violence escalates quickly and frequently recurs in the region’s most conflict-affected areas, with outbreaks occurring most recently in the Special Geographic Area and parts of Maguindanao del Sur. 17 An ambush on Bangsamoro’s Chief Minister Macacua in the village of Bitu in Maguindanao del Norte by unidentified gunmen further highlighted the region’s volatility. The attack did not hurt anyone in Macacua’s convoy. Edwin Fernandez, “BARMM chief survives ambush in Maguindanao”, Inquirer , 16 August 2026. Criminal activity in the Bangsamoro also thrives wherever state authority is weak. While petty crimes such as theft or robberies are relatively rare in the region, illicit economies are ubiquitous, and have evolved in parallel to the peace process. 18 Crisis Group interviews, observers and police officers, February-March 2026. Kidnappings for ransom, which used to be Mindanao’s most lucrative business, have almost disappeared; smuggling, however, has proliferated, including for goods ranging from weapons to cooking oil. 19 Maritime Bangsamoro in particular, especially the provinces of Tawi-Tawi and Basilan, along with its former province Sulu, has traditionally been Mindanao’s “backdoor”, where many local communities have long treated smuggling to and from the Malaysian state of Sabah as legitimate commerce. In Central Mindanao, illicit cigarette trading has also flourished, much of it supplied from Indonesia and Vietnam and allegedly shielded by local powerbrokers. Crisis Group interviews, Cotabato City, 9 February 2026; diplomats, Manila, 30 April 2026. See also, United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime, “ An Interconnected Criminal Ecosystem: Transnational Organized Crime Threat Assessment for South-East Asia ”, July 2026, pp. 216-217. This illicit activity, however, has not led to open violence between competing criminal interests as syndicates appear to work with local governments rather than against them, and turf wars are scarce. Human trafficking across the region, especially involving women, also remains a concern given the region’s porous borders and long coastlines. 20 See for example, Lean Bolongon, “Safeguarding minors: Combating illegal recruitment in BARMM”, Philippine Information Agency , 17 March 2026. Another profitable business in Mindanao is the drug trade. During former President Rodrigo Duterte’s term in office from 2016 to 2022, the Philippine police carried out a nation-wide anti-drug campaign that targeted suspected dealers and users, killing thousands. 21 Georgi Engelbrecht, “Philippines: The International Criminal Court Goes After Duterte’s Drug War”, 17 September 2021. While some Mindanao drug lords were killed, other networks survived and have since flourished. 22 Crisis Group interview, security analyst, Manila, 10 March 2026. As early as 2023 – just a year after Duterte left office – a local activist in Marawi declared that the “drugs are back”. 23 Crisis Group interview, Marawi City, 26 October 2023. The Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency and the police continue counter-narcotic operations; some locals say they have recently seen an increase in arrests and shoot-outs. 24 Crisis Group has recorded at least ten such anti-drug operations across the region in 2026 so far. One clash in August between security forces and an armed drug trafficking outfit in Bongao town in Tawi-Tawi left one person dead and three others wounded, including a naval officer. 25 Edwin Fernandez, “PDEA agent, drug suspect killed; 3 Marines wounded in Tawi-Tawi”, Inquirer , 9 August 2026. In the Bangsamoro, as well as in other regions where the state’s security apparatus is weak or corrupted, guns are viewed as symbols of status and power. The proliferation of firearms has also contributed to conflict and crime in the region. 26 It is notoriously hard to determine the total number of guns in the region. In late 2024, the police estimated that the region had over 27,000 unregistered firearms, while a well-informed interlocutor told Crisis Group that there were 20,000 legally registered ones. Crisis Group interview, 11 February 2026. In the Bangsamoro, as well as in other regions where the state’s security apparatus is weak or corrupted, guns are viewed as symbols of status and power; decades of war have made weapons ubiquitous. 27 Individuals and clans carry a wide variety of weapons, ranging from antiquated rifles to machine guns. Other Philippine regions where guns are prevalent are Abra and Negros. Members of armed groups and many local politicians, civilians and ex-combatants carry these weapons. 28 The first armed movement in the region, the MNLF, despite having splintered into factions, also retains weapons. The 1996 peace agreement with the movement sidestepped the question of disarmament, but in the absence of any attacks on government forces by a MNLF faction since 2012, Manila tolerates the awkward status quo of hundreds of MNLF fighters still being under arms. Crisis Group interviews, MNLF political cadre, Cotabato City, 16 February 2026. Under the 2014 peace agreement, the MILF has taken part in the gradual demobilisation of its forces. In early 2026, however, the group stopped formally participating in the process and other normalisation activities such high-level meetings due to Manila’s perceived failure to fulfil promises of socio-economic benefits for combatants who lay down their arms; 14,000 fighters have still to be decommissioned, along with 2,450 weapons. 29 Taher Solaiman, “MILF declares ‘temporary pause’ in peace process engagement with national government”, Luwaran.com , 17 March 2026. Following discussions between its peace panel and government counterparts, the MILF ended the temporary suspension of its engagement in the peace process in early August, but demobilisation of rebels appears to still be on hold. 30 Carolyn Arguillas, “GPH-MILF Peace Implementing Panels finally meet; MILF’s ‘temporary pause’ lifted”, Mindanews , 5 August 2026. While there has been a proliferation of Philippine gun laws over the past five decades, they are strikingly permissive. Under a so-called Type 5 licence, for example, Filipinos are allowed to possess up to fifteen firearms. Existing ordinances, moreover, are loosely enforced. Individuals often acquire weapons legally but then remove their serial numbers, making them untraceable. 31 Crisis Group interview, police officer, Manila, 10 May 2026. Consequently, the government’s main focus is on the pool of “loose” firearms – those guns which the state cannot trace or document – with the goal of either seizing them or persuading politicians and civilians to turn them in. 32 The term “loose firearms” refers broadly to weapons that rebels, criminals or civilians hold without proper registration, including those purchased legally but later left unregistered or with expired licenses. But the task is overwhelming; civil society activists say guns continue to flow in and out of the Bangsamoro without any means to trace them. 33 Crisis Group phone interview, source from Basilan, 28 February 2026. High-calibre weapons such as mortars, machine guns or assault rifles can easily stoke local conflicts as their lethality increases the likelihood of casualties and tit-for-tat retaliation. 34 On 2 August, national police chief Jose Nartatez pushed for a crackdown on illegal firearms and armed groups in the region ahead of the September polls. Andrea Gregorio, “PNP ramps up ops vs gun-for-hire groups ahead of BARMM polls”, Inquirer , 2 August 2026. For its part, the interim regional government has only recently started discussing a bill to regulate firearms and ammunition in the autonomous region. 35 Member of parliament Omar Sema filed the bill on 16 April 2026, marking the sole instance that such legislation has been discussed in the regional parliament, out of the 469 bills it has passed so far. In the meantime, local governments such as the province of Basilan have launched programs to collect small arms and light weapons. This effort is being done in coordination with the national peace process office and is underwritten by foreign donors. Buy-in, however, has been uneven. 36 An obstacle to these schemes is that the market value of firearms often surpasses the cash incentives offered to rebels or civilians for surrendering them. Two senior military commanders expressed deep scepticism about the campaign, arguing that the initiative would have no meaningful impact on the security landscape, was far too modest in scale, and targeted the wrong weapons (those not in the hands of rebels or ex-combatants). Crisis Group interviews, Maguindanao and Cotabato, February-March 2026. Other proposed solutions, such as forced mass disarmament or the comprehensive registration of firearms, do not seem realistic in the Bangsamoro context. 37 Crisis Group interviews, interim government officials and civil society representatives, Cotabato City, February-March 2026. Efforts to create “zones of peace” or “gun-free zones”, often initiated by non-government organisations, have been short-lived. 38 Crisis Group interview, head of a civil society organisation, Cotabato City, 9 February 2026. Policing under Autonomy To meet the challenge of the post-conflict landscape, the drafters of the 2014 peace agreement had to think hard about the best way to police the region. 39 During the peace talks, policing was a key subject – as contentious as it was during negotiations between the government and the MNLF in 1996. That peace agreement contained no provisions for disarmament or demobilisation, and clashes continued to flare more than a decade after the deal. While the 1996 agreement envisaged integrating MNLF rebels into state forces, only a quarter of the insurgent force eventually joined the police or military, voluntarily bringing with them more than 4,000 firearms Crisis Group interview, military officer, Manila, 26 February 2026. See also, Miriam Coronel-Ferrer, “Integration of MNLF forces into the PNP and AFP: Integration without demobilization and disarmament”, unpublished paper for UP Center on Integrative and Development Studies project on the GRP-MNLF peace agreement, 2000. The agreement called for a regional police force that was to be “civilian in character, effective and efficient in law enforcement, fair and impartial, and accountable under the law for its actions”, and whose mandate would be “law enforcement and maintenance of peace and order” in the region. 40 Framework Agreement on the Bangsamoro and Annex on Normalisation . But the division of labour between Manila, its national police force and the region remained ambiguous. 41 The Philippine National Police, created in 1991, is tasked with preventing and investigating criminal activities and strengthening internal security. The Department of Interior and Local Government has political control over the force, while the National Police Commission (NAPOLCOM) administers and disciplines it. The president selects the national police chief and senior police officers and appoints the secretary of the department of interior and local government. Headquartered in Manila, the force maintains regional, provincial and municipal stations across the archipelago, but also includes two specialised units: the Criminal Investigation and Detection Group focuses on organised crime and terrorism; the Special Action Force, the PNP’s elite commando unit, is in charge of counterterrorism, hostage rescue, and high-risk operations as well as ad hoc tasks such as patrolling hot spots during elections. One part of the agreement stipulated that the regional government, working in coordination with Manila, “shall have primary responsibility over public order and safety within the Bangsamoro”. 42 Annex on Power Sharing , Art. II, 14. In another part, the accord said the police force is “responsible both to the central government and the Bangsamoro government”. 43 Framework Agreement and Annex on Normalisation. The Philippine Constitution is clear in that regard, as Art. 10 Section 21 states: “The preservation of peace and order within the regions shall be the responsibility of the local police agencies which shall be organised, maintained, supervised, and utilised in accordance with applicable laws. The defence and security of the regions shall be the responsibility of the National Government”. Government officials involved in the negotiations say the agreement was clear the regional police would remain under national authority. 44 One official involved in the process, however, said that Manila dodged the hard questions until the end, keeping the wording intentionally vague, and ended up “parking” the issue for the future. Crisis Group interview, Manila, 31 July 2026. The MILF, however, maintains that the common understanding in talks was that policing should be under the control of the autonomous government. The agreement also set up an Independent Commission on Policing to determine how law enforcement should function in the new region. When the commission delivered its report in April 2014, it recommended that the force remain a part of the national police, but stressed that it should invest in community‑based policing. 45 The Independent Commission on Policing for the Bangsamoro, “Policing for the Bangsamoro”, 2014. Report on file with Crisis Group. Community policing is generally understood as an approach that builds active partnerships between law enforcement and local citizens to solve community problems and jointly ensure public safety. The commission highlighted the need for community policing that respects human rights and Sharia law. Another problem the commission identified was the police’s weak accountability to the communities they serve. Tasked with translating the occasionally vague peace agreement into clear and legally binding terms, the 2019 autonomy law dismissed the idea of a separate Bangsamoro police force. Wary of clashing with the 1987 constitution’s centralised approach to policing, lawmakers assigned public order and safety to the national government. 46 A single national police force was mandated to curb the historical misuse of local law enforcement by warlords. Yet mindful of the authoritarian practices during Martial Law under Ferdinand Marcos, the constitution balanced this by granting local governments a supervisory role to ensure checks and balances. This outcome reflected the stance of former President Rodrigo Duterte, who was in office when the autonomy law came into force, but both the national police force and lawyers were also sceptical about proposals for a separate regional police force. 47 Crisis Group telephone interview, analyst, 18 February 2021. In early 2019, the national police established a Police Regional Office (PRO-BARMM), which is part of the national police and therefore firmly under Manila’s control. 48 According to most observers and local figures, any change to this status quo needs constitutional amendments. Crisis Group written communication, 12 June 2026. See also, Nash Maulana, “‘BARMM police, Moro Senate seat require Charter change”, Manila Standard , 3 May 2026. At the same time, the organic law included two compromise provisions. The first one was to allow the integration of MILF and MNLF members into PRO-BARMM (see Section III.A.2). 49 The MILF was critical towards integration of their forces into the police during the peace talks. Later, however, the movement accepted this provision in the autonomy law. The second one called for the chief of the regional police force to be appointed “upon consultation with the Chief Minister”. In practice, however, it is the national police chief who has ultimately decided on this appointment. 50 Crisis Group interview, government official, Manila, 27 February 2026. In late 2025, however, a national police commission resolution reiterated that the region’s chief minister can both recommend candidates and provide feedback on shortlisted officers. III. Security and Justice in Transition Various bodies in the Bangsamoro region are responsible for tackling flare-ups of violence. While the police and military remain central to maintaining order, other government and community institutions also help dispense justice and mediate disputes. A. The Police during the Bangsamoro Transition As is the case with the national police as a whole, the Bangsamoro force is hierarchical in nature. Its regional headquarters are in Parang, from which it oversees five provincial headquarters and more than one hundred municipal police stations. Every town has a team of officers who mostly take care of basic law enforcement. These tasks include investigating crimes, preparing requests for warrants or subpoenas from the courts, dealing with minor offences and arresting criminals and insurgents. 51 Arrest powers remain outside the military’s purview, except in instances of “in flagrante delicto” where troops directly witness a crime. The number of officers in the region is, by many accounts, insufficient: a regular station typically has a staff of a bit over twenty, covering municipalities with populations as large as 25,000. Overall, the police force’s headcount stands at over 7,000. 52 Crisis Group interviews, police officers, Cotabato City and Parang, 6-7 August 2026. Every municipal police chief shapes the local force’s policies on everything from community engagement and collaboration with politicians to defining how to handle local conflicts. In the post-2019 transition period, the police has emphasised anti-drug operations and curbing the spread of illegal firearms. 53 Crisis Group interview, senior police officer, Shariff Aguak, 27 March 2026. These priorities stem from the national government’s priority of combating drugs, as well as community support for the campaign. 54 Crisis Group interview, senior police officer, Cotabato City, 6 August 2026. Given their limited numbers and lack of equipment, it has been more difficult for the police to address complex clan feuds, which can flare up without forewarning. In the most conflict-affected parts of Maguindanao, the police struggle to conduct even routine patrols, leaving law and order in the military’s hands. 55 A police chief from the region distinguished between “law enforcement”, for which the police is in the lead, and “combat operations” that are the domain of the military. Crisis Group interview, Cotabato City, 17 February 2026. A senior police officer said the force can take care of so-called “soft targets”, but still need back-up if the operation occurs in a “harsh” context. 56 Crisis Group interview, Shariff Aguak, Maguindanao del Sur, 27 March 2026. According to one regional bureaucrat, the police may be willing to take over internal security but is currently “not capable” of doing so. Crisis Group interview, Cotabato City, 11 February 2026. Perceptions of law enforcers vary. The police appear more connected to everyday life than the military because their stations are located near town halls, making them visibly present. Some officers have a genuine desire to help their communities. But for many young Moro men and women, becoming a police officer is more about acquiring a secure job than answering the call of duty. 57 Crisis Group interview, member of parliament, Datu Odin Sinsuat, 13 February 2026; academic, Marawi City, 27 March 2026. Some locals are also sceptical about the ability of the police to respond to incidents. 58 In Lanao del Sur, a civil society activist also observed the police are too slow to respond to violence. Crisis Group interview, Marawi City, 14 February 2026. Locals in predominantly non-Moro Indigenous communities also feel that law enforcement does not always respond to their concerns. 59 Crisis Group interview, phone interview, community leader, 6 December 2021; online communication, peace process observer, 17 August 2026. That said, several surveys show the police enjoy a degree of trust from local people. 60 Crisis Group interview, Manila, 20 March 2026. Surveys made available to Crisis Group. Other survey data suggests that many residents continue to look to local leaders and religious figures for security. Tatsuya Koyama, “Who Supports the Peace? A Survey of Postconflict Public Opinion in Maguindanao, the Philippines”, Journal of Current Southeast Asian Affairs , vol. 44 no. 3 (December 2025). At the beginning of the transition, many MILF commanders hoped community policing – namely, building partnerships between law enforcement and local citizens to ensure public safety – would become widespread. 61 Crisis Group interview, senior MILF commander, Cotabato City, 27 November 2019. The Philippine police have used civilian auxiliaries known as the Barangay Peace Action Teams (BPATs) and Civilian Volunteer Organisations (CVOs) that came closest to community policing. With police approval, BPATs may carry light firearms. CVOs focus on intelligence gathering, neighbourhood patrols, and emergency response. Officially unarmed, they may use weapons when supporting police operations, although in practice some mayors or village heads have been known to issue them firearms. Despite the support of international donors, however, and its inclusion in the Philippine policing doctrine, this approach never really gained momentum. 62 Crisis Group interview, donor official, Cotabato City, 11 February 2026. Police officers admit that resource limitations, understaffing and local politics complicate the work of fostering stronger relations with Bangsamoro communities. 63 Crisis Group interviews, Cotabato and Parang, 5-7 August 2026. Even so, some individual officers have been more proactive. A former police chief in Maguindanao, for example, instructed his officers to visit communities and engage residents on important concerns, at times accompanied by representatives from the judicial system. 64 This community outreach mostly relates to drugs and firearms use. Crisis Group interview, senior police officer, Shariff Aguak, 27 March 2026. As for efforts to integrate MILF fighters into the police force, as stipulated in the autonomy law (see Section II.B), these have so far had limited success. In 2019, the government waived height, age, and education requirements for five years to allow more former MILF (and MNLF) rebels to qualify for recruitment in the regional force. After a two-year interruption due to the COVID-19 pandemic, 11,075 applicants took a special eligibility exam in May 2022, which 7,145 passed. Yet in the years that followed, the government earmarked only about 400 positions for the former fighters, and just 396 joined the police force. 65 At present, 36 women were considered for recruitment and have undergone on-the-job-training in police stations across the region. “The Peace Accords Matrix – Mindanao (PAM-M) and Civil Society Normalization Update Report (January-April 2026)”, University of Notre Dame, 3 August 2026, p. 11. While the interim government stepped in to fund their training, Manila subsequently grew sceptical of maintaining dedicated quotas for ex-rebels, and future applicants will have to compete within the general pool of all Filipinos vying for the 1,500 police positions available annually. 66 Third Party Monitoring Team, 9th public report, 5 May 2026, p. 61. A small concession was a resolution by the national police commission in July 2025, which extended the police application deadline for MILF and MNLF members to 8 June 2027. Bong Sarmiento, “MILF, MNLF members who want to become cops can apply until June 2027”, Inquirer , 17 July 2025. While they may not have joined in large numbers, the former MILF fighters now working as police officers appear to have integrated smoothly. While they may not have joined in large numbers, the former MILF fighters now working as police officers appear to have integrated smoothly. 67 Crisis Group interview, Manila, international observer, 21 October 2022. Police officers from Cotabato City said MILF recruits have been well‑received by their new colleagues, and a sense of camaraderie now animates the ranks. 68 Crisis Group interviews, Cotabato City, 28 March 2026, 6 August 2026. The Third Party Monitoring Team – an independent body mandated with overseeing the peace process – has encouraged further recruitment, underlining it “could serve as a powerful symbol of previously warring entities working constructively to build a secure future together”. 69 Third Party Monitoring Team, 9th public report, 5 May 2026, p. 61. But prospects for further integration appear dim. Manila has demonstrated no appetite to reintroduce a quota for ex-rebels or hire Moro who passed the exam but were not incorporated into the force. A part of the MILF, furthermore, still expects the regional government to take over policing in the region in the long term. 70 Crisis Group interview, international observer, Manila, 14 October 2022. Crisis Group interviews, MILF officials, February-March 2026. In this sense, the policing issue is emblematic of a broader lack of agreement on the future of the peace process. 71 Crisis Group interviews, international and local observers, Cotabato and Manila, February-March 2026. Marking its new secretary’s first 100 days, the Philippine peace process office’s late-July report made no mention of policing.
