The Role of the Armed Forces While the region is immersed in a transition marked by ongoing episodes of violence, the superior operational capacity of the Armed Forces of the Philippines means that they remain in charge of most aspects of Bangsamoro security. In terms of force structure, the military has three infantry divisions across the region and two other divisions backing its northern and south-eastern flanks. 72 The 6th Infantry Division is in Awang, Maguindanao del Norte; the 1st Infantry Division in Pagadian, Zamboanga del Sur; the 11th Infantry Division in Jolo, Sulu; the 4th Infantry Division in Cagayan de Oro and the 10th Infantry Division in Davao City. Light infantry battalions are based in population centres, with companies deployed in key towns or villages. 73 A senior officer argued the military is the most visible manifestation of the state in some villages and enjoys more legitimacy than police, courts or local politicians due to better logistics, disaster response capabilities and ability to withstand clan capture. Crisis Group online communication, navy officer, 16 June 2026. Part of the military’s acceptability is also its commitment to the ceasefire with the MILF. To boost its reach, the military has also employed so-called force multipliers. These include paramilitary forces such as the Citizen Armed Force Geographical Units (CAFGUs). 74 President Corazon Aquino established CAFGUs in 1987 to help meet the challenges posed by communist and Moro insurgents. Aquino’s successor, Fidel Ramos, sought to scale back auxiliaries during the 1990s, but in 2001 President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo, confronted with mounting internal threats, expanded their ranks once more. Since then, CAFGU contingents have steadily grown. The CAFGU Active Auxiliaries serve fifteen days a month and are integrated into the army’s chain of command; the Special CAFGU Active Auxiliaries operations also fall under the formal authority of the armed forces but local governments or private firms pay for them to guard businesses or secure territory. From the perspective of the military’s central command, maintaining these auxiliaries – which have tens of thousands of members – is more cost‑effective than expanding the regular force. 75 At least one government official told Crisis Group there is a cap now on CAFGU recruitment in Mindanao. Crisis Group interview, Manila, 27 February 2026. In some conversations with Crisis Group, however, commanders still pushed for CAFGU recruitment. Observers also noted recent training in areas such as Lanao. Crisis Group interview, Manila, 15 March 2026. Critics, however, express concern about lack of discipline, and say these paramilitaries are at risk of becoming private militias answerable to kinship networks or to whichever group pays them. They also get involved in local land disputes, either as direct party to the conflict or at the behest of landowners. 76 Crisis Group interviews, civil society activist, Marawi, 26 October 2023; MILF member, Datu Odin Sinsuat, Maguindanao del Norte, 28 March 2026. The military’s priorities in the region have shifted over the last seven years. The military’s priorities in the region have shifted over the last seven years. At the beginning of the transition, especially in areas where insurgent and militant activity was concentrated, the military focused on high-value targets and combat operations, leaving the maintenance of “local peace” to the police. 77 Crisis Group telephone interview, security analyst in Sulu, 24 August 2021. As the threat level associated with militant groups decreased, relations between local residents and military personnel have improved. 78 In the past, communities were fearful of the armed forces, but the Bangsamoro peace process has altered that perception, even if many locals do not forget the military’s past abuses and heavy‑handed operations in their areas. A key task for the army has since become that of “managing” the MILF: while waiting for the decommissioning of the ex-rebels, troops need to control the fall-out of internal feuds emanating from the movement’s involvement in local politics. 79 Officers try to keep community disputes in check by supporting conflict resolution, though there are variations in how they go about this. Crisis Group interviews, military officers, Datu Odin Sinsuat, 16 February 2026. Concern about rebel resurgence shapes military commanders’ threat perceptions, but from the division level down to the battalion, officers maintain fluid communication channels with their MILF counterparts. 80 Crisis Group interviews, military commanders, Lanao and Maguindanao, January-April 2026. The peace agreement foresaw the military redeploying outside the Bangsamoro, a move that military leadership should now be keener to make given the country’s shift of focus toward external defence. 81 See Crisis Group Asia Report N°349, Riding Unruly Waves: The Philippines’ Military Modernisation Effort , 12 August 2025. But beyond existing “rotational rationalisation”, which happens on a regular basis, military leaders have been cautious about reducing their footprint in the region. 82 Crisis Group interview, Manila, 26 February 2026. Redeploying the military was part of the peace agreement but has made only limited progress. For one thing, residual violence persists in Mindanao. 83 Crisis Group interview, foreign military adviser, Manila, 29 May 2026. There are fears that a sizeable withdrawal would leave a vacuum, with neither reserve forces nor police ready to step in. 84 A military assessment said that “apart from the intensified checkpoint operations, the police must proactively target criminals and private armed groups that may influence the election process”. Report made available to Crisis Group. A regional bureaucrat admitted that given the reach and intensity of local conflict, it would be good “to keep the military where it is”. 85 Crisis Group interview, bureaucrat, Cotabato City, 15 February 2026. There is a legal reason for the hesitation as well. Philippine law assigns the military primary authority over combating internal threats; for the police to assume control, these laws would have to be amended. 86 Crisis Group interviews, security officials, Manila, 4 February 2026. Examples include Republic Act No. 8551 of 1998, which restored the military’s primary role in suppressing insurgency and internal threats while assigning a supporting function to the police, and the Anti-Terrorism Act of 2020, which gives surveillance and intelligence-gathering authority to both police and the armed forces. Members of the military – especially those in the army – also benefit from the current setup. Divisions and brigades wield not only military authority but also economic clout as they generate local jobs and may receive funds from local authorities. 87 Crisis Group interview, military officer, Manila, 22 June 2024. In addition, the armed forces’ current metrics for performance evaluation and promotion do not encourage a shift in priorities, with experience in counter-insurgency efforts still helping to boost officers’ career prospects. C. Law, Justice and Conflict Resolution The peace agreement and the autonomy law recognised that in order for the Bangsamoro to exercise self-governance, it will need a system of justice that reflects the region’s culture and values. The region’s citizens have various legal regimes to choose from. 88 Art. X of the Bangsamoro Organic Law . The regular Philippine judicial system functions through municipal and regional trial courts, ensuring access to common legal processes. These extend down to the community level, where the barangay or village justice system also provides a formal venue for resolving local disputes. 89 The barangay is the smallest unit of political administration in the Philippines, generally accounting for a cluster of villages. The village justice system, mandated by Philippine law since 1991, comprises local councils that are tasked with mediating disputes before they reach formal courts. Settling a dispute at the village level, however, does not guarantee it will not reignite. Crisis Group interview, Bangsamoro lawyer, Cotabato City, 5 August 2026. Moro and other Indigenous communities maintain their own justice practices. Rooted in custom rather than formal litigation, these systems remain outside direct government oversight yet enjoy the support of local people. Relying on individuals with no or minimal formal association with the state, these processes typically lead to amicable settlements. 90 Crisis Group phone interview, 17 August 2021. See also, Raihan A. Yusoph, “Hybridizing Justice: Cultural Legitimacy and the Limits of Traditional Dispute Resolution in Lanao del Sur, the Philippines”, Asian Journal of Peacebuilding , vol. 13 no. 2 (November 2025), pp. 207-230. Sharia, or Islamic law, also applies to Muslims in the region if they choose to submit to it. Under the supervision of the Philippine Supreme Court, several Sharia courts handle family matters and personal affairs, such as divorce or inheritance. 91 Ferdinand Marcos Sr. created Sharia courts in the Philippines in 1977 as a measure to curb the influence of the Moro rebellion in Mindanao. The peace agreement strengthened this type of jurisdiction. 92 While the MILF had originally envisioned a broader application of Sharia law, the autonomy law ensured the region’s jurisdiction did not extend beyond the Philippine constitution’s limits. Crisis Group interview, MILF official, Cotabato City, 9 February 2026. Some local MILF authorities, such as community camps or commanders, also maintain their own Sharia jurisdictions. 93 The MILF officially pronounced its Sharia courts dissolved a few years ago, but the informal system still functions in some areas. Sometimes, communities perceive the Sharia courts’ actions as overreach. Crisis Group interview, local civil society activist, Cotabato City, 15 February 2026. But views differ across the Bangsamoro as to the desired scope of Islamic law. Many MILF cadres would welcome Sharia as the main legal system. 94 Crisis Group interview, senior MILF commander, Datu Odin Sinsuat, 26 October 2022. Some non-MILF members also think Sharia could “decongest” cases for Muslims in public courts, and strengthen the rule of law among Moro communities. 95 Crisis Group interview, 11 February, source from Cotabato City, 11 February 2026. Other Moro Muslims, however, prefer the public court system, given that it is still the most official route and enforcement is at least formally guaranteed, over traditional mechanisms, which are perceived to be quick but less authoritative. 96 Crisis Group interview, Marawi City, 27 March 2026. Bangsamoro citizens use these different justice mechanisms – whether traditional mediation, Sharia or public courts – depending on the types of issues at hand, but also based on their class, gender or ethno-linguistic group. While in principle this “forum shopping” arrangement can be useful, problems arise if conflict parties such as former rebels, clans or insurgents fail to accept resolutions from these various judicial bodies, leading to disputes resurfacing and becoming more violent. [The] legal fragmentation makes Bangsamoro institutions offering routes to conflict resolution all the more important. This legal fragmentation makes Bangsamoro institutions offering routes to conflict resolution all the more important. The interim government has several bodies dealing with public safety, the most important of which is the Ministry for Public Order and Safety, whose mandate is to prevent and resolve clan feuds that have long destabilised the region. That said, the ministry’s small budget has left it with limited reach. 97 The Ministry for Public Order and Safety and some legislators have often channelled large sums to feuding clans as an inducement to settle. The ministry has also provided training to local community monitors. Initial hurdles at the outset of the transition, however, especially regarding the ministry’s precise mandate, and internal friction within the bureaucracy, have all hampered its effectiveness. Crisis Group interview, local analyst, 18 August 2026. In addition, as local conflict was rising around 2022, the chief minister created the Peace, Security and Reconciliation Office, whose mandate overlaps with the ministry but focuses more narrowly on disputes among MILF members. Leadership changes, however, have reduced the office’s effectiveness. 98 Crisis Group phone interview, analyst, 5 June 2026. Critics argue that the office’s impact has waned under the current director, Castro Emran, citing a perceived loyalty to the region’s chief minister over the MILF chairman, whose rival factions now compete with one another for political influence and mass support. More generally, many observers view him as less proactive in resolving issues than his predecessor, Anwar Alamada. Local government officials, meanwhile, constitute the first line of political authority, and are also crucial in dealing with outbreaks of conflict. They do this in two main ways. First, local mayors or village captains have the mandate to fix local disputes in their town or village. Secondly, they chair peace and order councils, which bring together officials, security personnel (including police chiefs and senior military commanders) and community representatives to coordinate responses when violence erupts. 99 Crisis Group interview, expert, M’lang, Cotabato province, 29 October 2023. Some councils meet regularly, thereby also playing a conflict prevention role, but others convene only after unrest has broken out. In many cases, the convening of the councils is a formality but does not make a dent on disputes. 100 Crisis Group interview, senior national security official, Manila, 25 March 2026. “They are often just talk shops”, quipped a military officer. 101 Crisis Group interview, Datu Odin Sinsuat, 28 March 2026. Finally, the peace agreement created Joint Peace and Security Teams – hybrid units comprising police, military and MILF personnel. While these are now deployed across 24 locations, they have limited mobility and only a few teams actually seek to manage conflicts. 102 Summary Report made available to Crisis Group, BARMM Peace Conference 2025, “From Consultation to Action – Advancing Peace Together”, p. 8. For instance, despite the presence of a team in parts of former Pikit town – a notorious conflict hotspot until a few years ago – a local noted that its effect on deterring violence or settling disputes is minimal. 103 Crisis Group interview, security manager of a non-governmental organisation, Cotabato City, 10 February 2026; local observer, Cotabato City, 11 February 2026. Some observers view their creation as purely symbolic – a confidence-building measure between Manila and the MILF, which is valued for their mere presence more than their real contribution. 104 Crisis Group interviews, local security analysts, Cotabato City, 9-10 February 2026. A local court building in Cotabato City, Philippines. August 2026. CRISIS GROUP / Georgi Engelbrecht IV. Overcoming Community Insecurity Despite – or because of – a complex web of overlapping peacebuilding institutions, the Bangsamoro region is struggling to deliver the payoff autonomy was supposed to bring. Multiple actors – including the police, regional ministries, and municipal governments – help keep the peace. This system reflects a desire to prevent any one entity from becoming too dominant. But in practice this diffusion of authority means the underlying sources of conflict often go unaddressed. A. Law Enforcement Challenges Policing in the region is complicated by a thicket of operational challenges. As stated previously, communities in the BARMM require more police than current resources allow. The region’s geography, which includes porous coastlines, rugged and mountainous terrain, as well as isolated villages, further slows operations and inhibits deployment. With units overstretched, municipal forces struggle to deter clan feuds and must often wait for military reinforcements. In addition, equipment and training gaps persist, from forensic capacity to the absence of high power firearms or even patrol cars. 105 Crisis Group interview, policing expert, Manila, 12 May 2026. Locals also allege that, despite their mandate to safeguard lives and property, police officers tend to neglect investigating crimes unless citizens formally report them. 106 Crisis Group interviews, local community observers, Lanao and Maguindanao, February-March 2026. Finally, when feuds erupt in communities, police officers sometimes hesitate to respond because they fear they and their families could be dragged into the dispute. 107 Crisis Group interviews, military commander and community members, Marawi City, 14 February 2026. Allegations of corruption further undermine the police’s effectiveness. Theft or illicit sales of police weapons and ammunition has meant that on occasion arms meant for law enforcement have ended up in the hands of those it seeks to fight. 108 In 2018, for example, more than a thousand Kalashnikov AK‑47 rifles that the Philippine National Police issued found their way to communist insurgents, leading to graft and falsification charges against senior police officers. See also, Barbara Dacanay, “Manila: Top ranking policemen accused of selling high-powered firearms”, Gulf News , 15 September 2018. Anecdotal evidence indicates that some police force candidates effectively purchase their positions, and may look for more economic payoffs once in their posts. Observers also noted that the drug war under former President Duterte left its mark on the police, both in shaping the institution – heavy-handedness has become the norm – and through the practice of reassigning underperforming officers to Mindanao. 109 Crisis Group interview, security expert, Manila, 2 February 2026. Police officers that are well-trained and have a solid grasp of the region, on the other hand, are not always tapped for their expertise by commanders in the national force. 110 Crisis Group interview, government official, Manila, 30 March 2026. Aligning law enforcement institutions with the peace process and ceasefires has proven far more challenging than it has with the military. Aligning law enforcement institutions with the peace process and ceasefires has proven far more challenging than it has with the military, which had more exposure to armed violence. This has resulted in several clashes between police and the MILF, as law enforcement officers failed to coordinate with the ex-rebels when conducting raids. More broadly, members of institutions such as the National Police Commission, and even senior police officers assigned to the region, especially when they are new, struggle to understand certain requirements of the peace process such as ceasefire protocols, largely because national authorities fail to properly explain to them why they matter. 111 Crisis Group interview, government official, Manila, 27 February 2026. Perhaps the biggest issue concerns the national police’s accountability. In the Philippines, political influence on the police extends across all levels, encompassing provinces, cities, and municipalities alike. This happens because local officeholders, whether mayors or provincial governors, are automatically deputised as representatives on the National Police Commission, which supervises the work of the force. Political influence comes in two ways. First, governors and mayors play a key role in selecting officers for the positions of provincial or municipal police chief. Secondly, officials also have the power to direct and oversee the day-to-day functions of police in their area. 112 Philippine law, through Republic Act 6975, grants local chief executives “operational supervision and control” over police units, defined as the authority to direct, oversee, and inspect their operations. Mayors exercise considerable financial influence by providing essential equipment and operational funds that the central government fails to supply, often making the national police dependent on local government support. In the worst case, police officers even end up taking part in local politicians’ so-called private armies. Powerful figures hold different perspectives on how – or whether – to deal with political influence on the police. Some members of the MILF and the bureaucracy clearly wish the police would have no ties with local politicians, whereas political clans and local officials, unsurprisingly, are keen to preserve the status quo. 113 Crisis Group interviews, Cotabato City, February-March 2026. Some military commanders Crisis Group spoke to also said that the police’s links to local politicians render the force “less effective”. 114 Crisis Group interview, commanders, Central Mindanao, February 2026. B. Fragmented and Politicised Institutions Another difficulty arises from the overlapping jurisdictions of the national government, the regional administration and local governments. Although the police and military are officially in charge of security, in practice the autonomous government – not to mention provincial and municipal authorities – often step in. This can result in all parties asserting responsibility, but only to the point they find convenient. For instance, even if regional guidelines on settling clan feuds are in place, personalities in localities where conflict erupts often matter more than institutions in curbing them. 115 Crisis Group interview, Cotabato City, 9 February 2026. In addition, while the regional government has some prerogatives (see Section III.C), it does not stand above the security forces’ chain of command. To borrow the words of a local clan leader, all this means that the regional administration only has a “semblance” of authority. 116 Crisis Group interview, Cotabato City, 26 October 2022. Mayors, on the other hand, shift between resolving local issues when it works to their advantage or passing the buck to higher authorities or the military when it does not. Another concern is the interaction between the police and the military, which sometimes compete for authority, at times giving rise to a “power play”, as an observer who has worked with both institutions put it. 117 Crisis Group interview, Crisis Group, 11 February 2026. Intelligence sharing between the armed forces and the police, for instance, has proven difficult, and the lack of clarity in the division of labour between the two forces can blur accountability to the state and citizens if operations go wrong. 118 Crisis Group interview, former senior military intelligence officer, 20 March 2026. Intelligence sharing is particularly problematic when the target of an operation has relatives within the police force. The Joint Peace and Security Coordinating Center, a mechanism established in 2010, is tasked with coordinating military, police and coast guard operations across the country. At present, however, it mostly focuses on convening meetings and information exchanges. 119 The national police chief has acknowledged that “initiatives must translate to visible action on the ground”. Christopher Lloyd Caliwan, “PNP, AFP, PCG boost operational capabilities amid evolving threats”, Philippine News Agency, 6 March 2026. Although local conflicts are on the rise, no regional institution appears ready to grapple with the fault lines within communities. 120 Crisis Group interviews, former regional official, Cotabato City, 26 March 2006; civil society activist, Cotabato City, 7 August 2026. There is little incentive for peacebuilding in the Bangsamoro while the MILF Central Committee, regional officials aligned with Chief Minister Macacua and clans (who run local governments) are distracted by the push to outmanoeuvre one another politically and campaign for elections. Some bureaucrats, for their part, are also affected by the MILF schism and hesitate to advance peace initiatives, fearing their efforts will either be ignored or exploited by higher-ranking officials. In parts of Maguindanao, for instance, settling clan feuds often serves as a vehicle for powerbrokers to cultivate influence over MILF commanders, rather than a genuine effort to resolve disputes. 121 Crisis Group interviews, sources from Maguindanao, Cotabato City, 5 and 7 August 2026. C. Shortcomings of the Justice System A flawed justice system further undermines police effectiveness since it corrodes the rule of law and creates incentives for people to take the law into their own hands. Memories of decades of conflict, regular bursts of violence and communities’ past experiences with state authority make it difficult to make the rule of law more than “an abstract concept”. 122 Crisis Group interview, civil society leader, Cotabato City, 26 March 2026. Furthermore, the area is not immune to violence directed at members of the judiciary, either to scare them away or exact vengeance. 123 See for example, John Unson, “Maguindanao’s deputy provincial prosecutor, 2 companions hurt in ambush”, Philippine Star , 21 February 2020. High-profile incidents have become more scarce in recent years. Public perceptions of the justice system are shaped by its slow pace. Public courts struggle with chronic understaffing and backlogs. Judges sometimes postpone hearings because they are overloaded with cases, rotate in and out of the region, or cannot travel safely to remote municipalities. For ordinary residents, going to court is a costly ordeal, requiring time and resources many do not have. Public Sharia courts, often considered alternative venues for justice, also do not have enough judges, prosecutors and lawyers, leading to delays. 124 Crisis Group interview, MILF cadre, 12 February 2026. Sharia judges need to pass both the conventional bar and Sharia examinations. Some Islamic law students in Mindanao see this as a hindrance. MILF courts also often fail to live up to expectations. 125 Crisis Group interview, Marawi City, 10 December 2019; legal expert, Marawi City, 13 February 2026. A big obstacle to a well-functioning judiciary in the Bangsamoro is that powerful elites profit from a compromised system. A big obstacle to a well-functioning judiciary in the Bangsamoro is that powerful elites profit from a compromised system. A police officer observed that influential local elites at times encourage the force not to file cases against criminals, and that courts often dismiss the charges if local powerbrokers are involved. 126 Crisis Group interviews, Maguindanao del Norte, 26 March 2026. A well-off member of an influential clan, for example, said that despite his closeness to a prosecutor, the court is not likely to initiate action over the murder of one of his clan’s members given the perpetrator’s family is equally, if not more, influential. 127 Crisis Group interview, Manila, 28 April 2026. The weak rule of law can also perpetuate conflict. For example in murder cases, members of smaller clans face the dilemma of whether to file a legal case, which can result in retaliation from their opponents, or retaliate themselves, which could spark a cycle of vendettas. As a result, families sometimes choose revenge over a tedious and cumbersome legal process. In other words, the “culture of impunity” associated with the decades of conflict still exists. 128 Crisis Group interview, Marawi City, 13 February 2026. A military officer with a long history in the region acknowledged that the justice system is “dysfunctional”. 129 Crisis Group interview, Marawi City, 14 February 2026. D. A Stopgap Peace A major challenge to peace in the Bangsamoro is the fact that security forces remain unable to stem the horizontal violence that plagues the region. The problem persists in part because they tend to manage localised conflicts rather than resolve them, leaving space for violence to resurface. When clashes erupt, in some cases violence continues for hours before the military, which is typically the first responder, steps in. Beyond the physical dangers that communities face, these experiences undermine public perceptions of the armed forces, and more generally of what peace should entail. 130 Crisis Group interview, source from Lanao region, Manila, 8 May 2026. The military has tried to develop more flexible rules of engagement that allow for the immediate separation of warring parties, resorting to force if necessary. These guidelines, however, have not been applied consistently. Typically, the military manages to strike a ceasefire between the clashing parties, but as it does not have the mandate to resolve the issue that triggered the violence, the conflict often reignites further down the line. A vital element in these arrangements is often the payment of “blood money”, a form of compensation offered following an individual’s violent death. Some politicians, and even members of the MILF rank and file, have come to view this practice as harmful, since payment offers no guarantee that the conflict will cease. There are other obstacles to hammering out durable ceasefires. As conflicts tend to spill over village and town boundaries, a broader solution dealing with root causes in several municipalities, such as land ownership disputes, would be preferable. Municipal governments, however, often struggle to cooperate, which means this approach often is not feasible. 131 Crisis Group interview, former regional official, Cotabato City, 12 February 2026. In addition, regional ministries sometimes apply “ready made” solutions they have already successfully tested elsewhere, without taking into account the local context of the feud they are dealing with. 132 Crisis Group interview, MILF leaders, Maguindanao del Sur, 28 March 2026. This has occurred, for example, in Maguindanao. There were also cases where no ministerial intervention followed at all and local people resolved the conflict on their own. Even the MILF is not always able to resolve feuds beyond achieving a ceasefire. 133 In one case, a MILF commander around the MILF camp Abubakar hesitated to resolve a land issue between two of his followers and advised the village to take care of it. There was, however, no follow-up. Crisis Group interview, land experts, Cotabato City, 11 February 2026. Furthermore, a local non-governmental organisation noted that “infrequent and unstructured” peace dialogues most often fail to include women, young people with disabilities and non-Moro Indigenous people. 134 Moro Women Development and Cultural Center, Inc., “From Consultation to Action – Advancing Peace Together”, Summary Report, Peace Conference 2025, Davao City, 4 December 2025, p. 30. In some instances, this lack of inclusivity has perpetuated feuding or revived land conflicts that had otherwise been considered as resolved. V. Pathways to Local Stability Addressing the complexity of local conflict in the Bangsamoro cannot be done through a single sweeping reform. Rather, it requires a series of careful adjustments across institutions. 135 Crisis Group interviews, police, military and local Bangsamoro officials, January-March 2026. Focusing only on the police or the judiciary is unlikely to produce the desired results, which is why regional stability hinges on a combination of different policies. Police outpost in Cotabato City, Philippines. August 2026. CRISIS GROUP / Georgi Engelbrecht A. Improving Security Coordination As the Bangsamoro stabilises, Manila has an opportunity to reorient its military toward external defence and set the foundation for the police to take the lead in managing day-to-day security in the region. While a full handover of responsibilities would be premature, the military and regional police can start formulating a plan to do so in the near future. 136 Crisis Group interview, police commission official, 12 February 2026. The existing Joint Peace and Security Coordinating Center (mentioned in Section IV.B) could be strengthened to take on this task. The centre should, for example, design more joint operations and establish a roadmap for regional and provincial security powers to be passed from the military to the police. Consolidating regional security will require a redistribution of state forces, while ensuring Mindanao retains a baseline military presence. 137 Crisis Group interviews, analysts, Manila, June-July 2024. The government should increase the police’s responsibilities in the region’s more stable areas, pairing this move with a gradual drawdown of military units. Mobile army platoons or detachments should deploy to volatile hotspots, including parts of Maguindanao del Sur, the mountainous corridor between Maguindanao and Lanao, and areas where non-Moro Indigenous communities live. To offset these small-unit redeployments, troops from the region’s flanks, such as the southern Visayas or eastern Mindanao, should shift to conflict-affected areas within the Bangsamoro in order to concentrate the military where it can maximise stability. Lastly, it is vital to deepen existing but modest military and police collaboration in Central Mindanao, through intelligence-sharing, joint training, and coordinated non-combat operations. 138 Crisis Group interview, senior military official, 16 February 2025. It is also crucial for the military to re-examine the rationale for auxiliary forces. In some areas that do not see conflict, some CAFGU paramilitary units should be demobilised. More broadly, better oversight of these forces is essential: commanders should apply strict accountability and disciplinary measures, and sanction transgressions. 139 Crisis Group interview, former military officer, Manila, 29 May 2024. In the long run, the Philippine government’s objective should be to dismantle all state-backed militias in a phased manner and rely only on professional forces. B. Reforming Regional Policing Reforming policing arrangements in a complex environment while remaining respectful of both the Philippine constitution and the Bangsamoro’s autonomous status will be difficult. As mentioned previously, Crisis Group takes the view that a Bangsamoro police force outside the realm of the national police is not practical at this stage. A more prudent approach in the short term is to reform the existing law enforcement set-up. 140 Crisis Group interviews, Lanao, Cotabato and Manila, February-March 2026. To that end, police stations must be resourced with the equipment they need. The national government should also hire more officers so as to boost the police-to-population ratio. Authorities could reassign qualified officers currently posted in peaceful areas outside the Bangsamoro to the region. They also could increase the recruitment of MILF and MNLF fighters into the regular police force, starting with those who passed the test but were never hired. Expanding the ranks of Moro officers would foster trust with both the MILF and with communities that still view the police with suspicion. Ensuring ex-rebel recruits receive proper training and mentoring, and are fully acquainted with the communities they serve, will be essential to prepare officers and cadets. Foreign donors involved with the peace process could support such initiatives with training design and funding. Adjustments in police operations could also help build a more credible force. Once it has the numbers and skills to do so effectively, the police should strengthen targeted deterrence in hotspots where clan feuds and community violence proliferate, combining surveillance, mediation and enforcement. It should also improve its intelligence gathering, including more information-sharing between police units and more efforts to question militants and individuals involved in feuding to understand the local drivers of conflict. Stepping up community policing would ... narrow the gap between police and the Bangsamoro public. Stepping up community policing would also narrow the gap between police and the Bangsamoro public. 141 Crisis Group interviews, police and regional government officials, Maguindanao and Lanao, February 2026. The regional police force should organise a new department that would recruit, train and deploy community safety officers. 142 Funding could come from the national or the regional budget, or a combination thereof. It should, however, bypass local governments and exclude their funding to prevent them from exerting undue influence. These would ideally be recruited among demobilised MILF rebels, and would be tasked with engaging local leaders and communities and conducting visible and non-confrontational patrols. They could also aid in criminal investigations. Before rolling this out across the Bangsamoro, Manila and the regional government could run a pilot project in some municipalities with independent monitoring of its progress. Here again, foreign donors could support such programs with targeted interventions. Lastly, to restore public trust, regional leaders should combat police corruption by enforcing existing regulations. The internal affairs service and other accountability bodies should reinforce such efforts through robust oversight. Tightening procurement and inventory controls is also essential to safeguard firearms and ammunition and prevent costly – and potentially dangerous – losses. C. Breaking Conflict Cycles Security reforms are vital, but quelling violence in the region will also require addressing longstanding conflicts. Regional and national authorities should strive to make local peace deals more durable and ensure stricter adherence to the rule of law. Curbing the proliferation of firearms will necessarily be part of that process. 1. Sustainable conflict resolution Tackling horizontal violence requires de-escalating tensions when they arise, preventing them from re-erupting, and addressing root causes through conflict resolution. To prevent local quarrels from morphing into full-blown firefights, security forces need to step in as early as possible. The army, police and MILF structures all have a role to play. While the military remains best equipped to quell firefights, particularly those involving clashing MILF (and possibly MNLF) factions, internal rifts within a single MILF unit are best mediated by the ex-rebels themselves. In case of minor incidents, relying on the mediation of trusted community figures would also help avoid escalation. Effective conflict resolution in the Bangsamoro should also reach beyond the rapid responses needed once violence breaks out to address the underlying causes of conflict. Initial ceasefire agreements should include clear protocols, including sanction mechanisms, laying out the next steps in case the conflict parties violate the terms of the agreement. Once ceasefires are in place, they require rigorous monitoring, whether through the deployment of nearby police and military units, or through the participation of informal community watchers – a mechanism that has already proved successful, for example last year in the case of some feuds in Datu Saudi Ampatuan and Mamasapano towns. 143 Crisis Group interviews, local mediators, Datu Saudi Ampatuan, Maguindanao del Sur, 28 March 2026. 2. Building inclusive justice The police may be the “first face of justice”, but the broader judicial sector needs to be reformed as well. 144 “Policing for the Bangsamoro”, op. cit., p. 18. A first task is to strengthen the courts. This should happen through better staffing and the provision of security guarantees for judges and prosecutors, particularly when it comes to accessing remote areas. Public Sharia courts also need more support, which could come in the form of training for MILF members who are currently judges in their respective communities, but wish to practice in public courts as counsellors. 145 Sharia counsellors are individuals who passed a Sharia legal exam administered by the Supreme Court. They can represent clients and practice law at public Sharia courts. Increasing the number of so-called “mobile courts” – whereby representatives of the judiciary visit far-flung areas where there are no tribunals – would also strengthen the standing of the judiciary. In the same spirit, the regional government should broaden access to the justice system for its most vulnerable citizens by subsidising legal fees and travel expenses for community members who need to go to court. 146 Crisis Group interview, legal official, Cotabato City, 5 August 2026. Encouraging state institutions to coordinate more closely with bodies engaging in customary practices such as community mediation would also increase the efficacy of the justice system. Courts and other institutions such as village justice systems can reap the benefit of these customary practices by formally recognising not just traditional mediators, but also the actual settlement agreements reached thanks to them. 3. Navigating the firearms conundrum Dealing with the proliferation of weapons is also imperative. To begin with, the government and the MILF should restart the decommissioning of firearms. Getting the MILF back onboard with this process requires the government to deliver the support it promised demobilised fighters in the 2014 peace accord. 147 The Annex on Normalisation stipulates that in exchange for disarmament, the national government will implement a variety of other measures including compensation for demobilised fighters and the economic development of MILF camps. Given the need for the government and the MILF to rebuild trust and overcome the current stalemate, a realistic timeline will require that the process continue after the September 2026 parliamentary elections. Beyond the MILF’s weapons, the government should address gun violence in Mindanao. That begins with getting a better picture of the number of firearms in circulation. In addition to credible estimates of guns in the hands of insurgents and ex-rebels, the military and police need updated inventories of firearms issued to police and military auxiliaries, as well as clear guidelines on the storage and safeguarding of their weapons so that leaks do not occur in the first place. The state should also disarm police or members of military auxiliaries who take part in conflicts or abuse their power, and dismiss them. For their part, national agencies must tighten controls on smuggling, imports and domestic manufacture of illegal guns, as well as strengthen oversight of gun licensing and weapon registration. Across all interventions, authorities should prioritise the confiscation of high-calibre firearms, given how lethal they can be. Deterring actual gun use is also critical. Establishing a highly visible and competent police presence should serve as the foundation for these efforts. To maximise impact, these police deployments ought to be combined with strict firearm bans across the region in the lead up to elections, when gun violence tends to peak. 148 The police said that until early August they arrested twelve persons for violating the gun ban. Joviland Rita, “PNP: 12 arrested for violating BARMM election gun ban”, GMA News , 3 August 2026. Authorities should also impose penalties not only on those who possess unlicensed firearms but also those who manufacture, store or use them for political ends. Religious leaders and clan elders can also contribute to eradicating the excesses of Bangsamoro’s gun culture by mounting campaigns to rectify the belief that the use of firearms beyond self-defence is legitimate. 149 Crisis Group interviews, local civil society, Cotabato and Marawi, February-March 2026. VI. Conclusion Armed rebellions have tailed off across the southern Philippines, but the peace they have given way to is constantly threatened by clan warfare, political volatility and factional disputes within the former insurgent MILF. The architects of the Bangsamoro peace agreement saw reforms to the police force, backed by improvements in institutions handling conflict resolution and justice, as a way to propel the region from war to peace. Yet a series of obstacles has slowed police reform and prevented institutions from maintaining law and order. Manila and the Bangsamoro government will need to work in tandem and be realistic about proposed reforms. A law enforcement system that is competent, representative and fair, and which can earn public trust by making communities safer, is an essential step forward. A more effective and accessible judicial system, as well as moves to tighten gun control and ensure that peacebuilding initiatives address the social and political undercurrent that lead to fighting, are also vital. These reforms would not only contain violence but also signal that the region’s institutions are catching up with its aspirations for peace. Somalia’s End-of-year Cliffhanger pzeiler Thu, 09/03/2026 - 16:47 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Podcast / Africa 03 September 2026 1 minutes Somalia’s End-of-year Cliffhanger This week on The Horn , Alan talks with Samira Gaid, founder and senior analyst at the Mogadishu-based think tank Balqiis, about the possible end of UNSOS, the UN logistics operation supporting African Union troops and Somali government forces fighting Al-Shabaab and what may come next. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Related Tags Somalia In this episode of The Horn , Alan is joined by Samira Gaid, founder and senior analyst at the Mogadishu-based think tank Balqiis about the U.S. decision to oppose renewed United Nations logistical support for the 19-year-old African Union military mission in Somalia. Samira explains why UN logistical support has been critical to the AU mission as well as to Somali government forces fighting Al-Shabaab, and why its loss could leave some areas outside Mogadishu increasingly vulnerable. They also discuss what could happen if no solution or stopgap measure is found, and the 12,000-strong African Union mission ceases to function by the end of the year. They discuss how such a scenario could shift the balance of power on the battlefield between the federal government and Al-Shabaab. They also assess whether Mogadishu’s pursuit of bilateral security partnerships could fill the void left by a weakened or defunct AU mission. This episode is produced in partnership with the Friedrich-Ebert-Stiftung. Click here to listen on Apple Podcasts or Spotify . On Our Radar eschelhaas Fri, 09/04/2026 - 00:00 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Special Coverage / Global 04 September 2026 20+ minutes On Our Radar On Our Radar scans conflicts and crises around the globe every week and features some of the hotspots Crisis Group’s analysts are closely watching. Whether an under-reported trend or a headline-grabbing development, our field experts explain why it matters or what should be done. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Friday 4 September HAITI Armed gang members stormed the commune of Kenscoff, overlooking Port-au-Prince, overnight on 23-24 August, killing at least 47 people and abducting more than 50, whom they threatened to kill if security forces go after the gang in that area. At least thirteen abductees have subsequently been released. Briefing the UN Security Council on 28 August, UN envoy Carlos Ruiz Massieu said the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF) would beef up its presence in the capital, while Haitian units would send reinforcements to Kenscoff. He also urged the GSF, which remains far short of its planned 5,500-person strength, to deploy in full without delay. Crisis Group expert Diego Da Rin says the Kenscoff massacre is the latest indication that gangs are on the offensive as the GSF assembles. U.S. - IRAN After a month-long lull, the U.S. resumed attacks on Iranian soil over the weekend, first striking rocket launchers on Larak island that Washington said were preparing to deploy sea mines, then hitting dozens of military targets along Iran’s southern coast. Tehran responded with missile and drone fire at bases hosting U.S. forces in the Gulf. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says the uptick comes as the Trump administration tries to isolate Tehran financially through increased sanctions and a naval blockade, while in parallel undermining Iranian efforts to control the Strait of Hormuz by escorting vessels through the waterway. While Washington's approach is to squeeze wherever possible and strike whenever it deems necessary – for example, in response to Iranian strikes or efforts to rebuild its military capabilities – the Islamic Republic could counter with additional strikes of its own on U.S. assets and allies, along with further attacks on shipping. THAILAND Overnight on 22 August, militants in Thailand’s three southernmost provinces staged over 50 attacks in four hours, including bombings and arson attempts at local administrative offices, shops and other buildings. Three passersby were injured. Further incidents followed on 23 and 29 August despite tightened security. Authorities blamed Barisan Revolusi Nasional Patani Melayu (Patani-Malay National Revolutionary Front, BRN), which has fought Bangkok’s rule since 2004. Such coordinated attacks are routine, says Crisis Group expert Matt Wheeler, but the scale of this campaign was unusual. It was likely intended to discredit the state, demonstrate insurgents’ reach and heighten pressure on the government to resume peace talks that have occurred intermittently since 2013. Thailand’s chief negotiator has reportedly proposed bringing technical-level talks with BRN forward from October to this month, in part to determine the reasons for the attacks. 21 August 2026 CHINA - SOUTH KOREA Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi paid a two-day visit to South Korea this week to discuss bilateral ties, Korean peninsula tensions and broader Asian affairs. The trip came three days after U.S. President Donald Trump ordered the Pentagon to scale back joint military exercises with South Korea. Trump also said he is willing to meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, as he did during his first term. These two unilateral announcements in turn prompted South Korean President Lee Jae-myung to reiterate his call for Seoul to bolster its own defences, for instance by acquiring nuclear-powered submarines and regaining independent control of its military in the event of hostilities. (Its forces would now be under U.S. command in a wartime contingency.) Crisis Group expert William Yang says the U.S.-South Korean friction has given Beijing an opening to deepen its own engagement with Seoul. It may now seek to present itself as the main mediator on the Korean peninsula, given its links with Pyongyang. ISRAEL - SYRIA Israeli warplanes bombed the Abu al-Duhur air base in northern Syria early Tuesday morning, in what Israel said was a warning against “deployment” of Turkish military personnel at the site. No casualties were reported. In remarks protesting the strike, Syrian Foreign Minister Assad al-Shaibani said Turkish officers had visited the base three days previously, but only for “training” purposes as Syrian forces refurbish the base. Tom Barrack, the U.S. ambassador to Türkiye who doubles as envoy for Syria, described Israel’s action as “unnecessary”. The backdrop, says Crisis Group expert Noah Bonsey, is an impasse in Israeli-Syrian talks about a bilateral security agreement. Humanitarian needs also remain acute amid aid shortfalls; the Rafah crossing with Egypt has opened, after a long wait, but deliveries are still tightly restricted. Crisis Group expert Mairav Zonszein says the latest violence underscores how tenuous the ceasefire remains despite formally entering its second phase, when the sides are supposed to begin addressing issues of long-term security, governance and reconstruction. Diplomats need to press Israel to release its chokehold on Gaza and push for continued progress on the truce’s terms. PAKISTAN Police backed by soldiers reportedly killed more than 200 Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) fighters in raids throughout Balochistan, a south-western province next to Afghanistan, over the course of this week. The operations followed a rash of BLA attacks on police stations, military installations and residential areas that claimed 50 lives (33 civilians and 17 state personnel) over the weekend. Islamabad accuses the Afghan Taliban of harbouring the BLA high command, which they also say gets financial and logistical assistance from Pakistan’s arch-rival India. Crisis Group Executive Vice President Richard Atwood says the high death toll among the Baloch separatist insurgents shows that authorities planned the raids carefully, with a view to keeping civilians out of the crossfire. But these events are bound to increase tensions between Islamabad and Kabul, which are already high following clashes between Pakistani and Afghan Taliban forces last October, and to further chill relations between Islamabad and New Delhi. U.S. - COLOMBIA Presidents Donald Trump and Gustavo Petro met at the White House Tuesday after months of heated rhetoric prompted by disputes over issues such as migration, counter-narcotics cooperation and the 3 January U.S. raid grabbing Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro. Amid these exchanges, Trump went so far as to suggest that Colombia, too, might be a target of U.S. military action. Crisis Group expert Glaeldys González Calanche says the meeting proved constructive, helping ease the tensions in the bilateral relationship and signalling that the two countries can continue working together to curb drug trafficking. The two presidents also discussed the tariff spat between Colombia and Ecuador, with Trump offering to mediate between these countries’ leaders. Resolving the immediate trade crisis could pave the way for stronger collaboration between Bogotá and Quito in fighting organised crime. 30 January 2026 COLOMBIA - ECUADOR The foreign ministers of Colombia and Ecuador met in Panama after a week in which a trade dispute escalated between the two countries. The standoff began last week, when Ecuador announced a 30 per cent tariff on Colombian imports, blaming Bogotá for insufficient action to stop drug trafficking along the shared border. Colombia retaliated with tariffs on Ecuadorian goods and a suspension of electricity exports. Ecuador then raised the fee for Colombian oil shipped through its pipelines tenfold from about $3 to $30 per barrel. Crisis Group expert Glaeldys González Calanche says the meeting indicates that the two capitals understand the dispute will hurt both economies as well as weaken both states’ ability to confront security challenges on the frontier. Rather than acting in isolation, the two should mount a coordinated cross-border response, which is likely to be more effective in fighting transnational criminal networks. IRAN U.S. President Donald Trump told Iran Wednesday that it risks "major destruction" if it fails to negotiate a nuclear deal with Washington. The ultimatum follows earlier warnings of U.S. intervention over the Islamic Republic's repression of protests. The U.S. has dispatched additional naval assets, airpower and defensive systems to the Middle East. Tehran – along with some of its non-state allies in the region – has threatened retaliation if attacked. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says Iran is unlikely to meet the White House's sweeping demands, which encompass nuclear, missile and regional concessions, raising the likelihood of confrontation at a time when the Islamic Republic already faces increasing diplomatic isolation, mounting economic problems and outrage at its brutal crackdown on dissent. SOUTH SUDAN The South Sudanese army announced Sunday it is launching a major offensive to recapture territory in Jonglei state that has been seized by opposition forces and allied militias since hostilities intensified in December. The UN warned this week that mass troop mobilisation and inflammatory rhetoric from senior commanders have significantly heightened the risk of violence against civilians. Crisis Group expert Daniel Akech says the escalation signals a clear slide toward full-scale war. The rapidly expanding conflict threatens to draw in neighbouring states, including Uganda, and to deepen South Sudan’s dangerous entanglement in the war in Sudan. 23 January 2026 DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO M23 rebels withdrew from Uvira, near the Burundian border, over last weekend, ending a tense month in which they controlled the South Kivu town. They had promised to pull out, likely due to U.S. pressure following a December summit in Washington between their main outside backer, the Rwandan president, and his Congolese counterpart. The Congolese army and allied Wazalendo militias re-entered Uvira this week, but in the interim chaos engulfed the town, with widespread looting and abuses against civilians, mainly by the Wazalendo. Of particular concern, says Crisis Group expert Richard Moncrieff, is the mounting ethnic tension in the area. The M23 insurgents, who portray themselves as defenders of the Tutsi people, took Uvira claiming that the Tutsi-related Banyamulenge living in town needed their protection. Primary responsibility for attacks on Banyamulenge residents lies with the Congolese authorities and their allies, but the rebels appear to have exposed these people to predictable retaliation after retreating. Another M23-aligned armed group, the Twiraneho, is involved in fighting around Uvira, also pointing to a pattern of inter-communal violence. GUATEMALA President Bernardo Arévalo declared a 30-day state of emergency Monday after inmates had taken more than 45 guards hostage at three prisons two days earlier. After the authorities regained control of one of the facilities, gang members outside jail killed ten policemen in retaliation. The state of emergency limits citizens' rights and gives state forces special powers such as making arrests without cause. It echoes the iron-fist approaches to public safety pursued by leaders in El Salvador and Ecuador. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says Arévalo, who won the 2024 election touting a progressive reform agenda but has since lost popularity, listened to demands from Guatemalans for a decisive response to an uptick in violent crime. If the measure delivers immediate results, it could help the president’s political standing. UGANDA Tensions simmered this week after the 15 January elections, which saw President Yoweri Museveni win another term with 71.65 per cent of the vote. The leading opposition candidate, Robert Kyagulanyi of the National Unity Party (NUP), rejected the result, alleging widespread fraud. He remains in hiding after dodging a police raid – staged for reasons that remain unclear – on his residence. The president's powerful son, army chief Muhoozi Kainerugaba, said on social media Tuesday Kyagulanyi would be treated as an "outlaw/rebel" if he did not surrender within 48 hours. (He later deleted this and other inflammatory posts.) Meanwhile, authorities charged more than 100 NUP members with involvement in election day violence. An internet blackout has made details of the incidents difficult to verify. The official death toll is twelve, but both Kyagulanyi and Muhoozi have cited higher figures. The government says ten died when its forces were attacked at an opposition legislator's home, a version of events sharply contested by others who were present. Crisis Group expert Meron Elias says the opacity of events, along with Muhoozi’s threats, will likely keep the political temperature high following the polarising vote. 16 January 2026 CUBA The bodies of 32 Cuban soldiers killed during the 3 January U.S. raid in Venezuela arrived in Havana Thursday. Cuba is facing considerable uncertainty after U.S. President Donald Trump on Sunday urged its government to “make a deal” or face the consequences, vowing that the U.S. would cut the Venezuelan oil supply to the island nation, which is heavily dependent on these deliveries for its energy needs. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says Washington appears to be calculating that a deepening economic crisis in Cuba will mobilise the masses to bring about the regime’s collapse. The Cuban regime retains a strong military and solid ties to Russia and China, however, and previously has not hesitated to crush dissent. GREENLAND Several European NATO members have deployed troops to Greenland, an autonomous territory of Denmark, to beef up infrastructure and carry out joint military exercises after U.S. President Donald Trump repeatedly stated that the U.S. intends to acquire the island, by force if necessary. Wednesday’s meeting among the U.S., Greenland and Denmark in Washington failed to resolve “fundamental disagreement” on Greenland’s future, according to the Danish foreign minister. With Europe already buffeted by Russia's full-scale war in Ukraine, says Crisis Group expert Olga Oliker, this crisis will have dire implications for the future of NATO and European security writ large if the U.S. does not back down. SYRIA Thousands demonstrated in the north east Tuesday against government forces’ expulsion of Kurdish fighters from Aleppo. Since the last Kurdish fighters left the city Sunday, fighting shifted eastward, raising the risk of sustained confrontation. In early January, the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) clashed with the Syrian army in Aleppo as negotiations to integrate Syria’s north east under central government control stalled. Crisis Group expert Nanar Hawach says Damascus cannot take the whole region militarily, but it will likely keep applying pressure on the SDF. The U.S., which supports both sides, has kept a ceiling on escalation thus far and should use its leverage to bring the parties back to the negotiating table. 9 January 2026 CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC Provisional results show that President Faustin-Archange Touadéra has secured a third term after general elections on 28 December. Two challengers – Anicet-Georges Dologuélé and Henri-Marie Dondra – have called for annulling the vote, alleging fraud, while the main opposition coalition boycotted the ballot, citing an uneven playing field. The disputed poll coincided with renewed violence in the south east. Fighters linked to the Azandé Ani Kpi Gbé (AAKG) – a Zandé self-defence militia – disrupted voting in Bambouti. Clashes then spread, including AAKG attacks on government forces around Zémio in early January. The AAKG was initially aligned with Bangui but later broke with the government after its rapprochement with a Fulani-led armed group that the militia accuses of encroaching on Zandé land. Crisis Group expert Fulbert Ngodji says the AAKG may be digging in to battle the state. Stability during Touadéra’s new term will hinge on promoting intercommunal dialogue in the south east, better integrating militias under army command, and reducing regional isolation through development and security reform. IRAN The falling value of Iran's national currency sparked demonstrations that since late December have grown into nationwide anti-regime unrest. The government has altered its subsidy policies but done little to dampen wider grievances. At least three dozen people have been killed as state forces crack down on protests that show little sign of slowing down. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says the Islamic Republic faces a major dilemma: it is neither willing nor able to adopt reforms that could meet expectations for political, social and economic change and on notice from U.S. President Donald Trump that outside intervention is possible if its repression intensifies. LEBANON Lebanon said it had passed a milestone in disarming Hizbollah, but the country’s fragile ceasefire deal with Israel remains imperilled. On Thursday, the Lebanese army announced that it had brought all weapons under state control in the southern area between the Litani River and the Israeli border. Israel immediately disputed the army’s assertion, saying Hizbollah retains military infrastructure in that region. Crisis Group expert David Wood says Beirut faces dangers ahead in any case. The army must soon move toward disarming Hizbollah north of the Litani, where the group refuses to comply – driving up the risk of internal discord. Yet Lebanese leaders also know that Israel will almost certainly respond to any hold-ups in disarming Hizbollah with severe military escalations, inflicting still more pain on their embattled country. Suweida’s Exam Standoff Triggers Fresh Clashes in Southern Syria pzeiler Fri, 09/04/2026 - 14:57 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Analyst's Notebook / Middle East & North Africa 04 September 2026 2 minutes Suweida’s Exam Standoff Triggers Fresh Clashes in Southern Syria Crisis Group expert Nanar Hawach analyses a week of tensions in the Syrian province as government forces and local Druze troops once again trade fire Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Nanar Hawach Senior Analyst, Syria Related Tags Syria Tensions soared in late August between the Syrian government in Damascus and local forces in Suweida , a Druze-majority southern province that has stood outside government control since fighting in July 2025 killed over 1,700 . The immediate trigger for the unrest came on 19 August, when Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa decreed that some 13,000 students in Suweida should sit school exams in government-held parts of the province north of Suweida city, rather than in the city itself. Students had missed the regular exams in June due to the prolonged standoff between Damascus and the de facto local administration led by Sheikh Hikmat al-Hijri, a Druze spiritual leader. His so-called “National Guard” troops control much of the province, having benefitted from Israeli strikes against Syrian government forces during the July 2025 turmoil. On 24 August, al-Hijri doubled down, stating that the Druze are “an integral part of Israel” and share with it “even in creed”, claiming religious kinship – comments that drew widespread criticism within Druze communities. His remarks were also the latest instance of al-Hijri implying Israeli support for a separatist agenda, which Tel Aviv has thus far refrained from endorsing. Two days later, the “Shahba Operations Room”, an armed group allied to the National Guard, announced road closures and objected to exams being held in villages it considers “occupied”. On 29 August, thousands of students nevertheless boarded buses organised under local initiatives in a bid to get to the exam centres, before forces allied with the National Guard attacked the vehicles and obliged them to turn back. Reportedly, no students travelling from Suweida made it to the exams. Clashes broke out that night as the National Guard and Syrian forces exchanged mortar and heavy machine-gun fire, allegedly killing two civilians and a fighter in the Guard. Each side accused the other of firing first, but neither side gained any ground and calm finally returned on 1 September. These latest troubles illustrate the risk that Suweida’s conflict, while seemingly frozen, could flare up at the slightest provocation. Damascus and Suweida are locked in a struggle over who controls the workings of the state and public services. For Damascus, holding exams in areas under its control is an exercise of central state authority; for Suweida ’s Druze leadership, it is a challenge to their aspirations for autonomy. The costs of this struggle are increasingly falling on Suweida’s residents: without access to resources and state services, public frustrations within the province are likely to grow. The episode should serve as a warning to all involved over the huge potential costs of any resumption of conflict. Damascus should take care to avoid further military build-up in the areas and continue to work with contacts in Suweida on pragmatic solutions to the problems thrown up by the standoff. While Damascus’s control over state resources has increased pressure on al-Hijri’s camp, applying them to rebuild trust with Suweida’s residents could ultimately prove a wiser course of action.
